PEṬAKOPADESA

SUMMARY

The one who directed me to undertake the revision of the Peṭakopadesa was the Venerable Nāyaka Thera Ellāwala Siri Saṅkhivāhitadhāna, the resident head of Molligoda Pirivena (Pūrvārāmaya). Around the year 1940, the Nāyaka Thera, instructing that the Peṭakopadesa should be edited and prepared for printing, also supplied an old book printed in Burmese script. Having accepted this charge, I—then studying in the senior class of the pirivena—together with the Venerable Udispattuve Somaratana Nāyaka Thera, incumbent of Vigolle Vihāraya in Barawardhanaya division of Mahiyangana district, who assisted me, began the work of transcribing the Burmese book into Sinhala script and commencing its revision. The only text available to us for this purpose was a single copy—corrupted in many places by scribal errors and confused throughout—of the book printed in Hansawati, Burma, in the year 1909.

Thereafter I made great effort to inquire whether there existed any Peṭakopadesa written in Sinhala script. Since the Peṭakopadesa is a text that ought to be included at the end of the Khuddaka Nikāya, many old libraries and their manuscript collections were examined and searched. Among the manuscript collections we came across, most ended with the Cariyāpiṭaka; in some collections, at the end, the Netti­ppakaraṇa and a treatise called "Anāgatabuddhavaṃsa" were also found. However, in none of the manuscript collections we encountered was the Peṭakopadesa to be found. From this it had to be concluded that the Mahāvihāra commentators did not include the Peṭakopadesa among the canonical texts, and that, unlike the Nettippakaraṇa, it was not regarded as authoritative.

Later, a few people informed me that there existed a Peṭakopadesa written in Sinhala script, and I had brought and examined a palm-leaf manuscript containing the Nettippakaraṇa and the Peṭakopadesa together, belonging to the library of the Saddharmodaya Pirivena Monastery at Walapola, Panadura. This proved to be a copy made from the same old text printed in Hansawati, Burma, in 1909. That text, confused page after page and riddled with scribal errors, was of no assistance whatsoever to the revision of the Peṭakopadesa.

There is also a Peṭakopadesa printed in Roman script. It was edited in the year 1949 by Mr. Arabinda Barua (Ph.D.) and published by the Pali Text Society of London, printed at the Lanka Daily News Press of the Lake House establishment in Colombo. According to that gentleman, for his edition he had access to several Burmese manuscripts and also one manuscript written in Sinhala script. It appears that this Sinhala manuscript was itself a copy made from the book printed in Hansawati mentioned above. This is because no Sinhala copy older than that one is readily available in the country.

xxi

He said that the Burmese and Sinhala copies he came across were extremely confused, and that the original texts for the quotations in the Petaka could not be found in full; therefore, abandoning the effort to purify this book, he had it arranged and printed as well as could be managed. In this edition, could it not be said that the original form of the Peṭakopadesa has — to some degree or other — been "altered"?

Nor does it appear that in the Tipitaka revision undertaken by the Jātavaṃsadhītikāraka monks of Burma for the commemoration of the "2500th Buddha Jayanti," there was any particular concern shown for "Peṭaka revision." It should be noted that those Elders had the edition of Mr. Arabinda Barua printed in Burmese script. It should also be said that nowhere has it been purified, since even the confused readings and quotations that have not come down to revision — even in the "Desanā Pāli" — are the same in both books.

(i) padavidhānaṃ va lakkhaṇaṃ — P.T.S. — padavidhāno va lakkheṇo — Ma. Ja. Saṃ.
(ii) paridesā — P.T.S. — pariḷāho — Ma. Ja. Saṃ.
(iii) atiyātā — P.T.S. — ahiyātā — Ma. Ja. Saṃ.

These are a few such instances.

**Peṭakopadesa: Meaning of the Term**

Since it is the vessel of the teaching (pariyatti) spoken by the Fully Enlightened One, the Dhamma and Vinaya are referred to as "the Piṭaka." The explanation (saṃvaṇṇanā) of the Piṭakas is called "the Peṭaka," and the instruction (upadesa) given for the explanation of the Piṭaka is called "Peṭakopadesa." The treatise expounding it is, by this designation, named "Peṭakopadesa."

**What was the intended purpose of the author of the Peṭakopadesa?**

The Peṭakopadesa is a treatise composed in accordance with the Nettippakaraṇa. However, the author gives special attention to presenting (further) elaboration on points of Dhamma that the Nettippakaraṇa did not elaborate upon.

1. The treatise begins by providing special elaboration on the teaching of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Here, it first makes clear the manner in which every word of the Buddha, taught from the attainment of Buddhahood until the Parinibbāna of the Fully Enlightened One — the ninefold-factored Sāsana — is contained within it.

2. The Sāsanapaṭṭhāna, as set forth at the end of the Nettippakaraṇa, is an exposition concerning sixteen (16) "categories of textual teaching" (sutta-dhamma-vagga), such as (1) the Saṃkilesabhāgiya Sutta and (2) the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta, and so on. The author of the Peṭakopadesa, taking the "Sāsanapaṭṭhāna" as the second stage (bhūmi), presents an elaboration concerning fifty-one (51) "categories of textual teaching."

xxii

3. (a) The third (Suttādhiṭṭhāna) bhūmi, which gives details regarding the fourteen (14) adhiṭṭhānas.

(b) The fourth bhūmi, called "Suttavicaya," which gives instructions on the elucidation of the meaning of the suttas.

(c) The fifth bhūmi, called "Suttasamuccaya."

(d) The exposition of "miscellaneous dhammas" (pakiṇṇaka dhamma) found in the seventh bhūmi, and

(e) The special details regarding jhāna-meditation etc. found therein —

these should be pointed out as "special features" of the Peṭakopadesa.

This also confirms the conclusion drawn that the Peṭakopadesa was written in order to present "explanations of the Dhamma" not found in the Netti-pakaraṇa.

The author

It is also clear from the passage appearing at the end of the Netti-pakaraṇa text — "ettāvatā samantā netti, yā āyasmatā Mahākaccāyanena bhāsitā, bhagavatā anumoditā" — which is considered to have been placed there by the elders who compiled the Netti, as well as from passages such as "Mahākaccāyanena niddiṭṭhā" (in the Sadhigaha-vāra section) and "tenāha āyasmā Mahākaccāno —" (in the Hāravihāra section), that this work too was taught by the great Arahant Mahākaccāyana. The Netti commentary also confirms this. He was indeed one of the great disciples of the Buddha, and according to the Etadagga Pāḷi, he holds the tenth position among those declared foremost in the ability to fully analyze, by way of meaning and phrasing, discourses given in brief.

The "Peṭakopadesa" too is a work of this great elder named "Mahākaccāyana." This is stated in the Peṭakopadesa itself —

"Peṭakopadese Mahākaccāyanena bhāsite
Ariyasaccavibhaṅgappakāsanā nāma paṭhamā bhūmi samattā"

(page 30)

Further, in the fifth and eighth bhūmis therein —

"Suvīrassa Mahākaccāyanassa Jambuvanavāsino
Peṭakopadese Hāravihāro nāma pañcamā bhūmi samattā —"

and so on is stated. (page 144)

Details regarding this "residence at Jambuvana" mentioned here are not found in earlier traditional literary works. The great Arahant Mahākaccāyana, who is accepted by the author of the Netti-pakaraṇa, was a brahmin's son from the Avanti country (in the Southern region).

There was also a great elder named "Mahākātyāyanīputra," who is considered to have composed the "Jñānaprasthāna," regarded as a great Abhidharma treatise of the Sarvāstivādins, a work thought to have been composed about 300 years after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa. Some ask whether this Peṭakopadesa could not also be a work of his.

xxiii

Whatever the identity of the author may be, there exists a strong similarity between these two texts. In both texts, the subjects mainly dealt with are the same topics, namely:

(i) The sixteen hāras,
(ii) the five nayas, and
(iii) the eighteen root-terms (mūlapadas) — these are they.

(a) "Soḷasahārā netti, pañcanayā sāsanassa pariyeṭṭhiyā, aṭṭhārasa mūlapadāni mahākaccāyanena niddiṭṭhāni" — "The Netti [has] sixteen hāras, five nayas for the investigation of the Teaching, [and] eighteen root-terms, set forth by Mahākaccāyana."

(Netti, page 2)

"Soḷasahārā netti, pañcanayā sāsanassa pariyeṭṭhiyā, aṭṭhārasa mūlapadāni kaccāyanagottena niddiṭṭhāni" — "The Netti [has] sixteen hāras, five nayas for the investigation of the Teaching, [and] eighteen root-terms, set forth by one of the Kaccāyana clan."

(Peṭakopadesa — page 4)

(b) In the fifth section called the "Hāravibhaṅga," the author of the Peṭakopadesa, in order to explain —

(3) the Yuttihāra,
(4) the Padaṭṭhānahāra,
(5) the Lakkhaṇahāra, and
(7) the Āvaṭṭahāra —

first quotes the very verses that were composed in the Nettippakaraṇa to set forth these hāras.

To show (6) the Catubyūhahāra and (10) the Vevacanahāra as well, he again presents the verses of the Nettippakaraṇa, but with only slight alterations.

(c) Among the summary (uddāna) verses of the eighth section (page 328), the first three verses are the very verses that occur in the Uddesavāra of the Nettippakaraṇa (Netti, page 6).

Likewise, the five (5) verses given at the end there are the very verses given in the Niddesavāra of the Nettippakaraṇa (Netti, page 10). Between these, there are only very minor differences.

From this it becomes clear that the Peṭakopadesa, both at its beginning and at its end, draws upon the Nettippakaraṇa.

However, I think this too ought to be considered:

The Nettippakaraṇa begins with a verse of homage, namely —

"Yaṃ loko pūjayati — sa lokapālo saha devehi namassati,
Tassetaṃ sāsanavaraṃ — viññūhi ñeyyaṃ naravarassa"

"He whom the world reveres — that Guardian of the World, whom even the gods together pay homage to —
his excellent Teaching, that of the best of men, is to be known by the wise."

That "Gotama" is indeed none other than the Lord Śākyamuni himself.

xxiv

The Peṭakopadesa begins thus:

"Tamo sammā sambuddhānaṃ paramatthadassīnaṃ
sīlādiguṇa pāramīppattānaṃ —" and so on.

Here the homage is to the many Buddhas.

Also, here the Dhamma details found at places such as "dasa vatthukā kilesā" (page 268), the paramparā paccaya — samanantara paccaya (page 102), and the paritthāra bhāra (page 136), and so forth, should be compared with the Dhamma contained in the Tipiṭaka. The editor should also examine these matters, bearing these points in mind as well.

Contents of the Text

In the Peṭakopadesa there are eight bhūmis (chapters). They are as follows:

1. Paṭhama-bhūmi — Ariyasacca-vibhāvanā
2. Dutiya-bhūmi — Sāsanapaṭṭhāna
3. Tatiya-bhūmi — Suttādhiṭṭhāna
4. Catuttha-bhūmi — Suttavicaya
5. Pañcama-bhūmi — Hāravibhaṅga
6. Chaṭṭha-bhūmi — Suttatthasamuccaya
7. Sattama-bhūmi — Hārasampāta
8. Aṭṭhama-bhūmi — Suttatthavibhāgiya

Summary Verses (Uddāna Gāthā)

At the end of each bhūmi, the Dhamma points, teaching passages, or verses contained therein have also been (again) summarized by means of uddāna (summary) verses. At the end of the (1) first, (2) second, (3) third, (4) fourth, and (8) eighth bhūmis, such verses are given in sequence, numbering 5, 21, 9, 1, and 8 respectively. However, in some bhūmis such (uddāna) verses are also found in the middle. The second bhūmi (Peṭaka — page 56) is one such place.

All these uddāna verses are a matter for the compiling elders (Dhamma-saṅgāhaka theras) to determine. However, in some bhūmis — namely, the (5) fifth, (6) sixth, and (7) seventh bhūmis — uddāna verses do not appear. Whether these were omitted or whether they are simply a matter of subject matter [is uncertain]. Other instances of such omission are also found. One such instance is found on page 294. Likewise, a place where things have become confused is also found once. Such an instance exists on page 215. And so on.

Points Requiring Examination

(a) In the seventh bhūmi (pages 302–304), the passage "sadisikehi suttavaṇṇanaṃ pāṭhaṃ" — for what purpose was it given? — this needs to be clarified.

XXV

(a) It appears that, like the Nettippakarana, the Peṭakopadesa too takes the Sutta Piṭaka alone as its authority. Among the eighteen root-terms (mūlapada) given identically in both works, one such term (no. 9) is "the unwholesome" (akusala). It is as follows:

1. Taṇhā          4. Dosa          7. Sukhasaññā
2. Avijjā          5. Moha          8. Niccasaññā
3. Thalāho        6. Subhasaññā   9. Attasaññā

According to the Theravāda Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the defilements (akusala) are tenfold, as shown in the Dhammasaṅgaṇippakaraṇa (Buddha Jayanti edition, Dhammasaṅgaṇi, p. 458). They are as follows:

1. Lobha          4. Māna          7. Thīna
2. Dosa           5. Diṭṭhi        8. Uddhacca
3. Moha           6. Vicikicchā    9. Ahirika, and
                                    10. Anottappa

According to the Theravāda Abhidhamma Piṭaka, "taṇhā" and "lobha" are simply two names for one and the same mental factor (cetasika). This shows that, in presenting the "root-terms of the unwholesome," it is the Sutta Piṭaka alone that has been taken as authority.

(i) Further, the Netti commentary states that the following verse was spoken in the Peṭaka, introducing it with "vuttañ-hetaṃ Peṭake" ("thus it is said in the Peṭaka"):

Yatra ca saṅkhārā hārā sampadamātā nāyanti suttantaṃ
khāyañjanā vīyipūputthā — sā hūmī hārassapāto —

It states that this verse is spoken in the Peṭaka. However, this verse is not to be found in the copy of the Peṭakopadesa before us.

(ī) Likewise it is stated: "Samādhi paṭipakkho kāmacchandassa, pīti byāpādassa, vitakko thīna-middhassa, sukhaṃ uddhacca-kukkuccassa, vicāro vicikicchāyā" — "thus it is said in the Peṭaka," meaning: concentration is the opposite of sensual desire; joy, of ill-will; applied thought, of sloth and torpor; happiness, of restlessness and worry; sustained thought, of doubt.

This is to be found (i) in the Vinaya-ṭīkā (p. 91), and (ii) in the Visuddhimagga (p. 104). However, it is not to be found in the Peṭakopadesa before us.

(u) The opening verse of the Dhammapada, which belongs to the Khuddaka Nikāya, is everywhere given as:

Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayā —
("Mind precedes all states; mind is their chief; they are made by mind.")

But in the Peṭakopadesa it is given differently, as follows:

Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manojavā —
(with "manojavā," "mind-swift," in place of "manomayā.")

(ū) In the Sutta Nipāta, in the Ratana Sutta, the root-text of the 2nd verse is:

Kiñcāpi seṭṭha kammaṃ karonti pāpakaṃ —

In the Peṭakopadesa this appears instead as:

Kiñcāpi sekkho'pi kareyya pāpaṃ —
("Even though one still in training [a sekha] should do some evil...")

We feel that these points deserve further examination.

xxvi

TOC

**1. First Ground**

In the Peṭakopadesa, what comes first is the first ground, named "Ariyasaccappakāsanā" (Exposition of the Noble Truths).

Unlike in the Ñāṇappakaraṇa, there is here neither a compilation-section (saṅgahavāra) nor the sections of statement (uddesa), exposition (niddesa), and counter-exposition (paṭiniddesa).

Only the headings —
(i) Noḷandāhāra,
(ii) Pañcavidhanaya, and
(iii) Avadhāraṇa-mūlapada —

are set out as topics (mātikā); and following upon these, taking as background the Blessed One's auspicious first discourse, the "Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta," it is clearly shown how the nine-fold teaching of truth stands established therein.

In accordance with this, the various teachings contained within the Dhammacakka discourse — namely the four-fold truths pertaining to what is to come (āyati-sacca-dhamma) and the attainment of the path pertaining to what is to come (āyati-maggādhigama) — are drawn out and analysed in their several forms. With the completion of this analysis of the truths pertaining to what is to come, this "First Ground" also comes to an end.

**2. Second Ground**

The second ground is named "Sāsanapaṭṭhāna."

Here is shown, together with illustrations, a detailed treatment of the fifty-five (55) topics (mātikā) raised concerning
(1) the suttas connected with defilement (saṅkilesa-bhāgiya), and
(2) the suttas connected with purification/distinction (vāsanā-bhāgiya).

However, at the end, the following are set forth and then rejected by means of six (6) illustrations:
(50) action whose result is experienced by oneself,
(51) action whose result is experienced by another,
(52) action whose result is experienced both by oneself and by another,
(53) action (kamma),
(54) result, and
(55) both action and result.

**3. Third Ground**

"Suttādhiṭṭhāna" is the third ground.

Here is given a detailed explanation concerning:
(1) greed,
(2) hatred, and
(3) delusion — the unwholesome mental factors;
(4) non-greed,
(5) non-hatred, and
(6) non-delusion — the wholesome mental factors;
also concerning
(7) body,
(8) speech, and
(9) mind — the three doors (dvāra);
and likewise concerning the five faculties (indriya):
(10) faith,
(11) mindfulness,
(12) energy,
(13) concentration, and
(14) wisdom.

By drawing out passages of the teaching contained in the Sutta Piṭaka together with illustrative principles, and analysing these nine topics of attainment accordingly, this ground too comes to be named "Suttādhiṭṭhāna."

xxvii

TOC

4. The Fourfold Ground

The fourth ground, called "Suttavicaya" (Investigation of the Discourse), explains the procedure by which the text that has come down should be properly expounded — analysed — and examined. It shows both how, just as the arising of unwholesome states occurs, so too the development of wholesome states takes place, and for this purpose it presents the manner in which the textual Dhamma (the Buddha's teaching) was handed down, giving here an explanation concerning the four great standards (mahāpadesa). Citing examples such as the Gosiṅga-sutta of the Suttapiṭaka and the Dvedhāvitakka-sutta of the Majjhima together with others, it examines whether the Dhamma of the Buddha as shown by others accords with this, the true Dhamma of the Fully Enlightened One — and in order to make clear the procedure by which the matching (concordant) sense should be taken, "Sutta-saṃsandana" (Comparison of Discourses) and "Sutta-vicaya" (Investigation of Discourses) are shown here.

5. The Fifth Ground

The fifth ground, called "Hāravibhaṅga," is this. The sixteen kinds of hāras (modes/guides) that occur in the Nettippakaraṇa are here also explained in detail, following the very same order.

In the Netti, the author, having first introduced each hāra (2) by a verse in the Niddesa section, then again makes it clear by giving examples (3) in the Paṭiniddesa section. The author of the Peṭakopadesa, however, has not followed this same order.

Here — in the Hāravibhaṅga section — the author both introduces each hāra by its opening verse and at that very point also supplies examples, thus completing the exposition. In this connection —

(3) Yuttihāra,

(4) Padavasanahāra,

(5) Lakkhaṇahāra, and

(7) Āvaṭṭahāra —

for the analysis of these, the very verses taken from the Netti for this purpose are used.

(1) Desanāhāra,

(2) Vicayahāra, and

(16) Samāropanahāra —

for the analysis of these, different (altered) verses are employed.

(6) Catubyūhahāra and

(10) Vevacanahāra —

these too are introduced using the verse from the Netti itself, but with slight modification. Among the rest of the hāras, however, no verses at all are used for their introduction.

6. The Jhaṭābhūmi (Thicket-Ground)

What is called "Suttatthasamuccaya" in the Peṭakopadesa is the Jhaṭābhūmi. Here an explanation is given concerning sixteen matters of Dhamma:

1. The Five Aggregates
2. The Eighteen Elements

xxviii

TOC

3. Dvādasāyatanāni — The Twelve Sense Bases
4. Cattāri Ariyasaccāni — The Four Noble Truths
5. Sattatiṃsa Bodhipakkhiyā Dhammā — The Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment
6. Avijjā — Ignorance
7. Vipallāsā — The Distortions (of perception, mind, and view)
8. Samatho — Calm (Tranquility)
9. Vipassanā — Insight
10. Alobho Kusalamūlaṃ — Non-greed as a Wholesome Root
11. Adoso Kusalamūlaṃ — Non-hatred as a Wholesome Root
12. Amoho Kusalamūlaṃ — Non-delusion as a Wholesome Root
13. Cattāri Vakkāni — The Four ... (Vakka)
14. Ekādasa Sīlamūlakā Dhammā — The Eleven Dhammas Rooted in Virtue
15. Catasso Ariyabhūmiyo — The Four Noble Planes, and
16. Nava Anupubbasamāpattiyo — The Nine Progressive Attainments

— these are the sixteen topics.

It is shown at the very outset that the Blessed One's Dispensation is gathered together in three ways, namely in (i) the Aggregates, (ii) the Elements, and (iii) the Bases. Following the headings given above, each point has been made clear in accordance with the relevant teaching. 7. The Seventh Ground

Here the largest chapter is the "Hārayampāta Ground." Here too, what comes first is a miscellaneous exposition concerning the practice of "Samatha and Vipassanā." From page 186 up to page 308 — both belong to the "Hārayampāta Ground."

First, taking up the verse beginning "Kāmesu Yantā — Kāma-saṅga Yantā" and so forth, it is expounded according to sixteen modes (hāra). In this way, taking a verse such as "Yadā dve ca puññāni pacināti" and separating it out according to the sixteen kinds of dhamma through the teaching of the suttas, it is made clear how that teaching is established by way of the sixteen modes (hāra).

**A Note of Gratitude**

Among the texts that ought to be studied in order to properly grasp the "Teaching of the Tathāgata," this Peṭakopadesa holds, like the Nettippakaraṇa, a place of special importance. This is because mention of this Peṭakopadesa is found even in works such as the Vinaya commentaries and the Visuddhimagga, among others. Yet it does not appear that the Peṭakopadesa was, for any long period, in actual use among the bearers of the Dharma here in Sri Lanka.

What proved far more laborious for us than rendering the Peṭakopadesa into our own language was the correction of its textual readings. The corruptions introduced on various occasions by careless scribes, together with the few corrected readings we ourselves, as editors, have arrived at, are abundant throughout this text...

**Peṭakopadesa**

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One

**1. The First Section**

Homage to the Fully Enlightened Ones, the supreme seers,
who have fulfilled the perfections of virtue and the other qualities.

1. Two causes, two conditions, for the arising of right view together with its supporting basis: the voice of another, and wise attention within oneself.

2. Herein, what is "the voice of another"? It is teaching, exhortation, instruction, and discourse on the truths coming from another, in conformity with truth. There are four truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Whatever teaching, explanation, exposition, elucidation, clarification, and setting forth there is of these four truths — this is called "the voice that conforms with truth."

3. Herein, what is "wise attention within oneself"? Wise attention within oneself is this: when one has heard the Dhamma taught by another, and then, without being carried away by the object, attends to it wisely — this is called "wise attention within oneself." The manner of this wise attention should be understood by means of a simile.

Just as a skilled man [an archer], having wiped away his sweat, having steadily and carefully taken aim at a small target with effort, attains proficiency in archery — by that same cause he attains skill afterward through wise effort. In the same way, attention directed, without distortion, to the teaching of the Dhamma concerning suffering, its origin, and its cessation is called "attention." This is called "wise attention within oneself."

4. This should be understood by two similes: one who has not heard before, and lacks prior instruction, falls into decline — "whoever among sensual pleasures is not free from passion," and so on. Two similes are to be applied: one wrongly carried out, and one rightly carried out through wisdom.

Herein, both "the voice of another" and "wise attention within oneself" are these two conditions. The wisdom that arises through the voice of another is called "wisdom born of learning" (sutamayā paññā). The wisdom that arises through wise attention within oneself is called "wisdom born of reflection" (cintāmayā paññā). These two kinds of wisdom should be understood, the first being dependent on these two conditions. These are the two causes, the two conditions, for the arising of right view together with its supporting basis.

As to "suttas that are common (sādhāraṇa)" – in these suttas the truths are shown as common [to the teaching], whether taken in forward order, in reverse order, or point by point. There, this is the beginning:

**22.** The world is enveloped by ignorance (they are called "those who do not know"),
Through stinginess and negligence it does not shine forth;
Smeared over with longing, given to greed –
This is the great peril of suffering.

Herein, ignorance and stinginess – this is the origin (samudaya). The great peril – this is suffering (dukkha). These two are called the truths: suffering and its origin.

"The fetter and the things that are fetters" – thus it is explained in the connected discourse (saṃyutta) dealing with this matter.

Herein, the fetter itself – this is the origin. The things that are fetters – this is suffering. These two are called the truths: suffering and its origin.

**Herein, how is it both suffering and cessation:**

23. For the monk who has fully understood and become calmed,¹
the round of birth and saṃsāra is exhausted,²
and for him there is no more renewed existence.

Herein, what was said — this is suffering. What is cut off through direct knowledge — this is the cessation of suffering. "The round of birth and saṃsāra is exhausted, and for him there is no more renewed existence" — this is the explanation. By these two truths: suffering and cessation.

"Monks, there are these two liberations: liberation of mind through the fading of lust, and liberation through wisdom through the fading of ignorance." Herein, what was said — this is suffering. What is liberation — this is cessation. By these two truths: suffering and cessation.

**Herein, how is it both suffering and the flood:**

24. Knowing this body to be like a clay pot,
setting this mind firm like a fortified city,³
one should fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom,
and guard what has been won, remaining without attachment.

Herein, the body that is like a clay pot, and the mind that is like a city — this is suffering. "One should fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom" — this is the flood. By these two truths.

"Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon that." Herein, "abandon that" — this is the flood.⁴ Those states that are not-self and are to be abandoned — form up through consciousness — this is suffering. By these two truths: suffering and the flood.

**Herein, how is it suffering, origin, and cessation together:**

25. Whatever griefs and lamentations there are,
and sufferings of many kinds in the world,
these arise dependent on what is dear;
when what is dear is not present, these do not arise.⁵

Herein, the griefs and lamentations, and the suffering of many kinds that comes to be out of affection — this is suffering. The affection itself — this is the origin. The removal of desire and lust, the non-occurrence of what is dear — this is cessation. By these three truths.

**22  Petakopadesa — Elucidation of the Noble Truths**

The wanderer Timbaruka asked: "Is it made by oneself, or made by another?" Whatever the inquiry may be — this is suffering. Those who, without resorting to these two [extremes], [follow] the middle way: "with ignorance as condition, formations [arise]" ... up to "with birth as condition, aging-and-death [arises]" — this indeed is suffering and its arising. Consciousness, name-and-form, the sixfold sense-base, contact; feeling, becoming, birth, aging-and-death — this is suffering. Ignorance, formations, craving; clinging — this is the arising. Thus this ["Is it self-made?"] is the inquiry; and by the utter wearing-away of what is taken up, suffering [ceases] — this is suffering, and this is declared to be its arising. "With the cessation of ignorance, the cessation of formations" ... up to "the cessation of aging-and-death" — this is cessation. These are the three truths: suffering, and arising, and cessation.

Thus the unwise one, having seen that bond and that view, seeks after it, [thinking]: "This bond belongs to me," and so grasps it as "mine." Thus he thinks: "By this virtue, or by this vow, or by this austerity, or by this holy life, I shall become a deva, or [attain] to the company of some deva" — thus [he reasons]. That is wrong view, and so he is one bound by wrong view.

But for one who is established in virtue, free from attachment indeed, the virtuous one rightly gives rise to right reflection on that virtue, [and reflects]: "This and that, through that (virtue), in this very life ends in enlightenment, or thereafter, having gone beyond and beyond, reaches the imperishable end" — thus it is said. "It is well understood that it leads to cultivation (vāsanā)" — this saying about cultivation is explained.

Then, being concentrated in the moral precepts, having abandoned the hindrances, he thereafter, by right view, direct knowledge, and vision, teaches the Dhamma. He attains the unshakable Nibbāna. Whether in the dispensation he attains unshakable Nibbāna, or whether he is of a single-seed nature (ekabījī) — [it may be either way]. Then there are two kinds of persons who attain the noble Dhamma: the faith-follower and the Dhamma-follower. Of these, the Dhamma-follower is superior to the faith-follower.

Then there are two [further divisions] among those who have arisen from exertion: the one of dull faculties and the one of keen faculties. Then, again, among these, there are two: the one of dull faculties and the one of keen faculties. Then, the one of keen faculties who has arisen from exertion is superior; and the one of dull faculties who has arisen likewise is inferior — these are called unequal. Then it is said that these unequal ones decline; and from those who have arisen from exertion, the one of the lower stage, inferior in attainment, is said to fall short of this ground — thus these are the lesser persons.

**42 Petakopadesa — on the types of persons**

Herein, what are they? There are three: one who understands immediately (*ugghaṭitaññū*), one who understands through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*), and one who needs guidance (*neyya*).

Herein, the person who is *ugghaṭitaññū*, with keen faculties, trains with little hardship, and having attained the fruit of stream-entry becomes the **one-seeder** (*ekabījī*) — this is the first fruit of stream-entry.

Herein, the person who is *vipañcitaññū*, with keen faculties, trains with little hardship, and having attained the fruit of stream-entry becomes the **one who goes from clan to clan** (*kolaṅkola*) — this is the second fruit of stream-entry.

Herein, the person who is *neyya*, with keen faculties, trains with little hardship, and having attained the fruit of stream-entry becomes the **one reborn at most seven times** (*sattakkhattuparama*) — this is the third fruit of stream-entry.

These three persons, by the diversity of their faculties, are established in the fruit of stream-entry: the *ugghaṭitaññū* becomes the one-seeder, the *vipañcitaññū* becomes the one who goes from clan to clan, the *neyya* becomes the one reborn at most seven times.

This is the Discourse on Penetration (*Nibbedhika-sutta*).

Now, as to attaining the fruit of non-return (*anāgāmiphala*):

Herein, the *ugghaṭitaññū* person who is sharp-facultied (*tikkhindriya*) — there are two kinds of persons: having attained the state of non-return, he becomes either one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval (*antarāparinibbāyī*) or one who attains final Nibbāna upon landing (*upahaccaparinibbāyī*).

Herein, the *vipañcitaññū* person who is sharp-facultied — there are two kinds of persons: having attained the state of non-return, he becomes either one who attains final Nibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī*) or one who attains final Nibbāna with exertion (*sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī*).

Herein, the *neyya* person, having attained the state of non-return, becomes **one whose stream flows upward, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm** (*uddhaṃsota-akaniṭṭhagāmī*).

By the diversity of faculties between *ugghaṭitaññū* and *vipañcitaññū*: the *ugghaṭitaññū* who is sharp-facultied becomes one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval; the *ugghaṭitaññū* who is dull-facultied (*mudindriya*) becomes one whose stream flows upward, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.

By the diversity of faculties between *ugghaṭitaññū* and *vipañcitaññū*: the *ugghaṭitaññū* who is sharp-facultied becomes one who attains final Nibbāna with exertion; the one who is dull-facultied becomes one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval; the *ugghaṭitaññū* of middling faculty becomes one who attains final Nibbāna without exertion.

The *vipañcitaññū* who is dull-facultied becomes one who attains final Nibbāna without exertion; the *vipañcitaññū* of middling faculty becomes one who attains final Nibbāna with exertion. The *neyya* becomes one whose stream flows upward, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.

The *vipañcitaññū* who is dull-facultied becomes one who attains final Nibbāna without exertion; the *vipañcitaññū* of middling faculty becomes one who attains final Nibbāna with exertion; the *neyya* becomes one whose stream flows upward, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.

Thus the five kinds of non-returner, together with the once-returner and the three kinds of stream-enterer — these are reckoned as "trainees" (*sekha*).

Herein, the *ugghaṭitaññū* person who is sharp-facultied, having attained Arahantship, becomes one of two kinds: one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) or one liberated through wisdom (*paññāvimutta*).

Herein, the *ugghaṭitaññū* person who is dull-facultied, having attained Arahantship, becomes one of two kinds: one liberated in mind (*cetovimutta*) or one who has direct experiential realization.

Herein, the *vipañcitaññū* person who is sharp-facultied, having attained Arahantship, becomes one of two kinds: a bodily witness (*kāyasakkhī*) or one who has arrived at right view (*diṭṭhippatta*).

Herein, the *vipañcitaññū* person who is dull-facultied, having attained Arahantship, becomes one of two kinds: one who does not attain final Nibbāna in that very life or one who attains final Nibbāna as it continues.

Herein, the *neyya* person, through the attainment accompanied by consciousness and understanding, comes to the realization of Arahantship — this being the accomplishment of right action together with tranquility. These are the kinds of Arahant.

**44 Peṭakopadesa — Ñāyappatthāna (Method of Reasoning)**

This is the fourfold teaching: that which partakes of defilement —pe— that which partakes of purity. Among these persons, the Tathāgata declares the tenfold power.

What is the tenfold?

Here, when the Blessed One had newly arisen [as Buddha], a certain deity requested him, asking: "May the Sugata teach the Dhamma." He, surveying [the world] with his supreme Buddha-eye, saw beings as of three kinds: those bent toward calm, those bent toward insight, and those without [such inclination].

Of these, one bent toward calm will know one thing thus: "I shall attain [absorption]"; one will know: "I shall attain final nibbāna as an unconscious being"; another will know: "I shall undertake [a further] attainment."

Of these, one bent toward insight will know: "I shall reach the noble attainment"; another will know: "I shall reach the attainment that is not noble."

Of these, one without [such inclination, but] rightly practising, will know: "I shall acquire the collection of calm"; one practising insight will know: "I shall acquire the collection of calm"; one rightly practising will know: "I shall acquire the collection belonging to insight"; one practising insight will know: "I shall acquire the collection belonging to insight."

These three, by the Fully Awakened One's own supreme Buddha-knowledge, [are known]: one will know: "These phenomena belong to one state"; and will proclaim it accordingly to him; another will know: "Awakening to this matter will come about for him through hearing it from another"; one who has not fully understood this will know: "Such and such a vision will not arise for him without the removal of that defilement"; and whichever particular distinctions he has not realized before, he will come to know them in due course.

When he, the Sage, teaches the Dhamma to beings in many ways and with manifold expressions, in accordance with the diversity of phenomena, that disciple who discerns correctly will know: "I shall grasp the meaning accordingly" — this is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).

And when that same disciple, through his skill in expressions, will know: "I shall master the various expressions" — this is the analytical knowledge of expression (niruttipaṭisambhidā).

**52 PETAKOPADESA — The Mode of Deliverance (Nissāraṇa)**

Standing firm in these grounds and powers, the Tathāgata teaches a fivefold teaching: that which is connected with defilement, that which is connected with the residue of habit, that which is connected with vision, that which is connected with development, and that which belongs to the stage beyond training.

Herein, whatever is the defilement of greed, its deliverance is non-greed. Whatever is the defilement of (wrong) view, its deliverance is non-delusion. Whatever is the defilement of misconduct, its deliverance is the three wholesome roots.

What are these three? These are the three kinds of mental misconduct: covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view (with its accompaniments).

Herein, the mental misconduct of covetousness sets up the bodily act of taking what is not given, and together with it, the concealment of everything taken; it sets up the verbal act of falsehood, and all manner of distortion and all manner of deception. All this, from the outset, is the root called "covetousness." In falsehood and in taking what is not given, the volition is that of covetousness.

Herein, the mental misconduct of ill-will sets up the bodily act of killing living beings, and together with it, all grounds for hostility, grounds for resentment, grounds for contempt and anger; it sets up the verbal act of slander and harsh speech. The mental misconduct of wrong view, together with its underlying inclination, brings about ill-will and wrong view.

For whoever, having grasped and cultivated wrong view — whether born of greed or born of hatred — is entirely founded upon wrong view: for this reason wrong view sets up the bodily act of frivolous talk, and sets up the verbal act of frivolous talk as well. These three are called the unwholesome roots of misconduct.

Whatever is covetousness, that is greed; whatever is ill-will, that is hatred; whatever is wrong view, that is delusion. By means of these, together with the eight kinds of [wrong] view, [misconduct] is set up. Among these three unwholesome roots, one gains abstention from the tenfold unwholesome [course of action]. Of that whole defilement of misconduct, the deliverance connected with the residue of habit should also be understood.

Herein, that which has been abandoned is described thus: "this is greed, this is hatred"; delusion too, when abandoned in the same way, is "this is greed, the swelling [of greed]." For this reason, in regard to those states, greed becomes manifest. Even so, that is unwholesome: this is ignorance — that which, regarding the four [aggregates] as form, [views it] as impermanent; form is non-self — thus for one who so regards it, it arises from ignorance: form is non-self, or non-self is non-self, or form from form is non-self.

"Not having abandoned the five enmities" means not having given up the five training-precepts; having thus pointed out the enmities, it is for this very reason that it is taught that "at the breaking up of the body [he] is called immoral" — this has been shown by stating the cause, having been set forth in this way.

"These are the fool's marks of folly: he is one who speaks badly, one who is wrongly trained, and one who performs evil deeds." Herein, whatever he strives to do by body or by speech, this is his performing of evil deeds. Likewise, whatever false speech he utters, from then onward, this is his bad speech. And whatever training-precept [he transgresses], [that] misconduct of mind is his wrong training. Endowed with these three marks of the fool, he experiences suffering and displeasure thereby; being unrestrained and without full understanding, he spends his time [thus]. Indeed it is in this way that, by reason of the ten courses of unwholesome action beginning with the killing of living beings, he experiences the suffering and displeasure that arise from that cause.

Furthermore, when he sees a thief being punished at the king's command, being deprived of life, it occurs to him thus: "Just as this one has been seized by the king, so too might I be; just as this one is being put to death, so too might I be put to death" — he experiences the suffering and displeasure that arise from that cause.

Furthermore, when the fool, having been overcome [by fear], thinks: "What will become of me in this world?" — he experiences the suffering and displeasure that arise from that cause. This is the cause of the fool's characteristics; thereby, at the breaking up of the body, he is reborn in hell. This is what is taught as the "basis for this teaching."

**84 Petakopadesa: The Standpoint of the Suttas**

**(3) And what is the standpoint of delusion?**

**5.** "Even reckoning by hundreds and by thousands of world-ages, one would go on wandering on; and still, though cast down, one would recall again what was cast."

**6.** "That by taking up formations without end one will make an end of suffering" — this is not how things are; no such principle exists.

This round of birth and death, entered upon from a beginning that cannot be traced, has ignorance as its cause. Whatever formations one sets going, these too arise "conditioned by ignorance" — that very not-seeing is ignorance; and it is taught as itself empty. In one who goes on carrying formations without end, there arises the view: "this is mine, this I am, this is my self" — this notion has come forth out of emptiness, and it is ignorance that has put forth ignorance. Thus, being so, it is to be understood as empty without remainder, shown in terms of its abode. It is this very point that the Teacher intends to show here — nothing else.

"Whatever ascetic or brahmin, monks, does not understand 'this is suffering'" — this is to be understood in terms of the Four Truths. That very non-understanding is suffering; this is its cause. Through not understanding, one constructs manifold formations — this is the origin. And that which one seizes as a standpoint of view and clings to, thinking "this alone is true, all else is wrong" — this too is the origin. And whatever is thereafter laid down as fixed — this is cessation. In this way too the Teacher has shown it: by way of cause, by way of origin, and by way of cessation.

This too holds as a rule common to all things: that from the very beginning they are to be understood as empty of a cause. As it is said: "Monks, a first point of this is not to be found" — nor is there anything that, once known, need be known further. And whatever one holds as "mine" — this is the root of the unwholesome: whatever is greed, that is greed itself; whatever is hatred, that is hatred itself; whatever is delusion, that is delusion itself. Thus these three roots of the unwholesome are to be examined from the very beginning — in this way it is to be shown, and in this way it is not to be shown. Likewise, monks, likewise: since from the very start nothing is grasped, the cause, the origin, and the cessation are to be shown thus. This is said in summary:

**7.** "Whatever is greed, whatever is hatred, whatever is delusion that overturns the Dhamma —
when one departs from these, no more does the bond arise — even as the moon wanes, phase by phase."

Nor indeed, monks, is this world to be shown otherwise than as thus described. This is the standpoint of delusion.

88 Peṭakopadesa — Sutta-conveying

(6) Therein, what is non-delusion-conveying?

10. "Wisdom indeed is cultivated in the world — that which leads to disenchantment, and that by which one rightly understands the exhaustion of birth and death."

"Wisdom indeed is cultivated" means by the wise. "Leading to disenchantment" means leading to Nibbāna, as it has been explained. "Rightly understands the exhaustion of birth and death" — here non-delusion is the cause; that by which one understands is the support; and the perception of birth and death is the factor. Thus non-delusion is shown as cause, as support, and as factor.

Herein, the three faculties [are to be understood]: the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of gnosis, and the faculty of one who has known. Therein, what is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"? Here, monks, a monk, for the sake of attaining the yet-unattained noble truth of suffering [and so for the other truths], generates desire, makes effort¹, arouses energy, exerts and applies the mind, strives. (Thus it should be done for all four noble truths.)

Therein, what is the faculty of gnosis? Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is, "This is the noble truth of suffering" (and so with the rest of the teaching) — this is the faculty of gnosis. Through the destruction of the cankers one becomes free of cankers — this is called the faculty of one who has known.

Therein, the wisdom itself is the cause. That by which, knowing, one knows and strives — that understanding is the support. That by which all the cankers are abandoned is the cause; the knowledge of the non-arising of things that have arisen and may arise is the support; and [the fruit attained] is the factor. Therein, "it is to be known by me" — this is the mind [applied], the energy aroused, "what was to be done has been done"² — this is the support. "There is no more of this state" — this is known, this is the knowledge of non-arising. Thus these are the three faculties. Non-delusion is shown as cause, as support, and as factor. These have been shown as the uncommon [factors].

Therein, what are the wholesome roots that are common [to all]?

"Monks, I shall teach you what is wholesome and what are the wholesome roots. Therein, what is wholesome? The Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, up to right concentration. Therein, what are the wholesome roots? Non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion."

Therein, non-greed is the cause. That by which calm [is produced]... concentration — this is the support of non-greed. Therein, non-hatred is the cause. That by which the three things are brought about — right speech, right action, and right livelihood — this is the support. Therein, non-delusion is the cause. That by which the two things are brought about — right intention and right effort³ — this is the support. These together make up the Noble Eightfold Path as the factor. And what is its liberation? Through the fading away of lust, liberation of mind; through the fading away of ignorance, liberation by wisdom — this is the factor.

Thus these three wholesome roots have been shown as cause, as support, and as factor. In this way the wholesome things that are common [to all] should be declared.

90 PETAKOPADESA — The Designation of the Discourse

Herein there are two, and there are three; this is the verse:

11. "The measured and the unmeasured, and arising —
the sage [who stands] beyond the remainder of becoming,
delighting within, concentrated —
[illegible] the arising of such states."

"Tulamatulañca sambhavaṃ" means: that which is reckoned as measured is "tula" (the measured); that which is reckoned as unmeasured is "atula." There, two things are weighed: gratification (assāda) and danger (ādīnava). One is the gratification in sensual pleasures, one is the danger in them; this is the escape (nissaraṇa) — thus one understands liberation (nibbāna).

By a lengthy method the unmeasured cannot be weighed; comparing one against another, by the highest standard it remains unmeasured. Then nibbāna, like a jewel that should not be destroyed, is truly unmeasured (atula).

That knowledge and vision which is the penetration (abhisamaya) of the wholesome — this is "not in vain" (amogha). That which shows [the process of] becoming — this is non-greed (alobha). That which "delighting within, concentrated" makes clear — the dispelling of confusion — this is non-hatred (adosa). Thus these three roots of the wholesome [are shown] — "the measured and the unmeasured arise" — this is non-delusion (amoha).

That which is the convergence that produces becoming is greed (lobha) — this is the cause. That which, internally, is connected with one overcome by ignorance — this is the outflow (nissanda). [Thus is shown] what proceeds [from it].

These three roots of the wholesome are pointed out by way of cause, outflow, and fruit.

In the same way there is proceeding and there is ceasing: by the roots of the unwholesome there is proceeding, by the roots of the wholesome there is cessation. In these three ways the convergence with the unwholesome is to be sought. That which is confusion with regard to states is pointed out — together with craving, with conceit, with wrong grasping of views, with the unwholesome, with doubt, with sloth and torpor; with envy and with stinginess, with shamelessness and with lack of fear of wrongdoing — these the wise should understand.

These [groups of] states are pointed out in the texts of the Dhamma; whatever defilement there is among these various states and terms, that convergence is to be sought out — this is defilement. It is neither greed, nor hatred, nor delusion. Just as these are the roots of the unwholesome, so too the wholesome [roots] are to be understood, each opposed to its corresponding defilement. This is the designation of non-delusion (amoha).

A teaching of dhamma is given - whether it be wholesome or unwholesome - that should be examined further. If, when so examined by you, it is found to be empty [of meaning], no other matter should be taken up for consideration. By two noble qualities, one defilement may be abandoned; or by one noble quality, [a given] defilement may be abandoned.

But even when examined in this way, if it is found to be empty, that too should be investigated; and however it is found to be empty, that should be investigated - in such a manner as it was shown in that very discourse it should be made known by means of that very discourse. When the noble qualities have been taught, the defilement [to be abandoned by them] should be taken up and examined thus: "Which defilement, it is said, has been taught here, and which noble quality has been taught here, should be understood by its reason. Is it the case that this defilement is abandoned by these noble qualities, or is it not abandoned by them? And does this noble quality here lead to the abandonment of that defilement?"

It is not the case that every unwholesome quality seeks its abandonment through every wholesome quality, nor that every wholesome quality seeks to abandon everything whatsoever. For example, loving-kindness (mettā) is wholesome and lust (rāga) is unwholesome - yet it is not that lust is abandoned merely because loving-kindness is wholesome and lust unwholesome; rather, it is specifically through loving-kindness that lust is to be abandoned - it is through the removal of the object/basis of lust that loving-kindness brings about its abandonment. In just the same way, whatever defilement is to be abandoned is to be sought out by means of the [corresponding] discourse, not by a quality not found in that discourse; it leads to the abandonment of all defilement [only] when, in that discourse, the noble quality taught stands as the direct opposite of the particular defilement - it is by that means that its abandonment is to be sought.

Thus, in whatever way a wholesome quality is taught, by the reasoning given in that very discourse, defilement is not to be understood as something left untaught; so too, the noble quality is to be shown, in that same great discourse, always according to this same method, and should be examined accordingly - namely: "Given that this defilement has been taught and this noble quality has been taught, does this noble quality indeed seek to abandon that defilement?" It should further be examined thus: "By what manner is this defilement to be abandoned, and by what manner has this noble quality been taught?" In whatever manner the noble quality has been taught, in that corresponding manner this defilement is to be understood as to be abandoned. For in some cases, one defilement is to be abandoned not through faith but through seeing (dassana) - and the state of faithlessness itself is to be abandoned, just as wrong view and ignorance are to be abandoned through seeing. But it is not the case that ignorance is always to be abandoned through seeing alone; there is a dhamma that is to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā). In just the same way, for the manifestation of liberation through the removal of the conceit "I am," it is abandoned by the specific means proper to it, through an undistracted, well-composed mind (cetovimutti). In this manner the distinction should be examined further: that which is to be abandoned through seeing - in respect of that, the noble quality is taught in the manner proper to seeing. That which is to be abandoned through cultivation - in respect of that, the noble quality is taught in the manner proper to cultivation. That which is to be abandoned through practice/resort (paṭisevanā) - in respect of that, the noble quality is taught in the manner proper to practice. Likewise, that which is to be abandoned through removal (vinodana) - [it is taught accordingly]. As long as a being retains the taints (āsava), as long as faith is lacking - so long is that faithless state itself a dhamma to be abandoned...

**[On examining whether a teaching is genuine Dhamma]**

The noble Dhamma has been taught by [certain persons/sources]. That noble Dhamma should be examined. If it is Dhamma, it should be examined for; however it is taught in various ways, by that one it should be examined — should that teaching be approved or not, that should not simply be accepted. If it is not approved — if it is not found [to agree] — it should be tested against what has been heard [i.e. against the Suttas]. Whatever is tested and is found to agree, that should be taken; whatever, being tested, does not agree, that should not be taken. [In such a case one should conclude:] "Surely this was not spoken by the Blessed One; it has been wrongly learned by the venerable one [who reports it]." Thus it should be pointed out by means of the Great References (Mahāpadesa) — [and conversely, if it agrees, one should conclude] "This was indeed taught by the Blessed One, just as it has come down."

Whatever Dhamma is taught — whether it concerns what is wholesome or unwholesome — the source (or occasion) of that Dhamma should be sought out. For without seeking out the source, no proper access [to understanding it] arises. Here are the ways in which the source should be sought:

Here, a monk without having investigated declares, "This is Dhamma, this is the source" — this should be examined. What is meant by "source" here may be illustrated [by a simile]: [just as] a soft seed [grows into] a soft [plant] — likewise here the source, being soft, [produces] a soft Dhamma — this should be understood. But by what means is the source said to be impure? By the surrounding/attendant source and by the source belonging to a similar kind of circumstance. That source, being soft, should not be rejected as valueless. Why is this? Because even in an inferior source, something of inferior but genuine value, or the reverse, may be found. "All formations are impermanent" — this is a question to be answered categorically. "What is suffering, that has the arising of suffering as its cause" — this is a question to be answered by counter-question. "Is suffering the self?" — this is to be set aside. Thus in joy, delusion's snare is wrong view, ignorance is the covering snare; from that, from that very wrong view, the four taints (āsava) arise — the taint of sensuality and the taint of becoming, the taint of views and the taint of ignorance. From there, standing on that other view, delighting among the five kinds of sense-pleasure is the taint of sensuality; craving that arises for future existence is the taint of becoming. Then pursuit of the formless is the basis for the taint of sensuality and the taint of becoming; pursuit of the form-realm is the basis for the taint of views and the taint of ignorance.

Then, non-attachment is the cutting-off of the taint of sensuality; wisdom belonging to the higher training is the cutting-off [of the taint] relating to mental formations. [Right] knowledge is the cutting-off of the taint of becoming; non-clinging and supreme [vision] is the cutting-off of the taint of views; thorough examination of dhammas together with clear comprehension is the cutting-off of the taint of ignorance.

These four taints are the condition for the four kinds of clinging (upādāna): the taint of sensuality [is the condition] for clinging to sense-pleasures; the taint of becoming for clinging to [views of] becoming; the taint of views for clinging to views; the taint of ignorance for clinging to the doctrine of self — it is explained that these arise as conditions in this way.

Then the taint of ignorance is the condition for [confusion] regarding the body; for one who has that, there is the contemplation of body in body. The taint of views is the condition for [confusion] regarding phenomena; for one who has that, there is the contemplation of phenomena in phenomena. The taint of becoming is the condition for craving; for one who has that, there is the contemplation of feeling in feeling. The taint of sensuality is the condition regarding the five kinds of sense-pleasure; for one who has that, there is the contemplation of mind in mind.

Then from the contemplation of mind, the noble truth of suffering comes to be; from the contemplation of feeling, the various kinds of feeling occur — pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and whatever states of defilement arise in dependence on these, these occur among beings. From the contemplation of body, cessation comes to be; from the contemplation of phenomena, the path comes to be.

In these four [establishments], standing [thus], one grasps this view in this way — first: "Uppannāloke pamuditānaṃ cittaṃ āsavā" — [showing] that the arising of the taints there has that very origin; suffering, cessation, and the path have arisen because unwholesome dhammas have thus ceased to continue, there being no further occasion for the unwholesome. Then, having thoroughly comprehended, one who has fully understood in this manner dwells having overcome and gone beyond these defilements. This much is the brief statement made here regarding this matter.

**126 Peṭakopadesa, Fifth [Division]**

Thus happiness too should be investigated as a [wholesome] dhamma, and unwholesome dhammas by way of Conversion. This is the summary of the hāra of Conversion: "The four perversions are likewise to be reckoned — the path leading to the arising of self-identity, and the path leading to the cessation of self-identity."

**8.** What, then, is the hāra of Distinction (Vibhatti)?

Whatever requires being distinguished is called the hāra of Distinction. For instance: when something has arisen, a person takes it up again; having taken up what had arisen, he distinguishes it fully and completely, saying "this one, and this other." This is called the hāra of Distinction.

**9.** What, then, is the hāra of Reversal (Parivattana)?

Whatever is a statement made in terms of its opposite — this is called the hāra of Reversal. As was said by the Blessed One: "For a person of right view … knowledge arises" — this is to be understood [by seeing it set against its opposite], together with the whole of its context. This is called the hāra of Reversal.

**10.** What, then, is the hāra of Synonyms (Vevacana)?

**14.** "The synonyms are many, proclaimed for a single dhamma;
one who understands through what he has learned, skilled in voidness —
he is the one called the hāra of Synonyms."

For example, concerning the Venerable Sāriputta, with regard to a single matter, these are synonyms declared by the Blessed One: "Sāriputta is of great wisdom, of joyous wisdom, of swift wisdom" — this is a set of synonyms for wisdom (paññā).

And just as in the Analysis of the Path each factor of the path leading onward is pointed out by its synonyms, so too there are synonyms for ignorance. One and the same unwholesome root is known under this or that name in this or that region.

For indeed that same thing is called by various names in various places: that which is called "sensual desire" in the saying "for one who delights in every kind of sensual desire" is, in another saying, called "craving," as in "craving is the weaver that binds"; and that very same thing is called "dust" in the saying "the one who fills up with dust is purified." Thus, whatever dhamma is being taught, one should examine it thus: "Of what dhamma is this the name? Of what is this a synonym?" For when, in various places, one and the same thing is pointed to under different terms, each according to the context in which it is taught — in that way the synonym should be sought out. This is the hāra of Synonyms.

11. How is that analysis of wisdom accomplished?

Having taught the discourse "These are the Four Noble Truths," he lays down, firstly, the Truth of Origination in brief. "In the dark-complexioned world, there is food" — thus there is disease, thus there is craving, and so on. He sets forth wisdom with regard to that which should be understood, [in detail] ... up to ... abandoned.

"In the dark-complexioned world there is food; there is no disease ... up to ... he sets forth the wisdom of cessation."

"Her craving for sense-pleasures is here rooted out, her craving for existence is here rooted out, her craving for non-existence is here rooted out" — thus he sets forth the wisdom of abandonment. "Craving, by which one is led on, turns about through wisdom" — in this verse he sets forth the wisdom of mental application [or: of what is agreeable to mind]. Thus the Blessed One sets forth one single thing by way of the wisdom of mental application.

Now, since craving is the origin of suffering, it is on this basis that craving-as-origin should be shown in brief. As it is said: "When a thought of sensual desire arises, one does not tolerate it, one abandons it, one dispels it" — thus is the wisdom of elimination set forth.

Thus, among the states so classified — whether wholesome or unwholesome — whatever state arises dependent on that very state, and that very state passes away, that state should be understood as being conditioned by that [preceding state]...

That is the proximate cause of lust, hatred and delusion among the five aggregates, [namely] the feeling-aggregate. There are three feelings. Of these, pleasant feeling should be understood together with joy (somanassa); painful feeling should be understood together with displeasure (domanassa); neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling should be understood together with equanimity (upekkhā).

And whatever is felt — that is the truth of suffering, [and it is] included in the formations-aggregate. Here the body is the measure by which it is reckoned, [this is] called "that which is bodily formation." Formation should be understood as twofold: by way of wisdom there are meritorious formations, non-meritorious formations, and imperturbable formations — these are stated as causes. When lust is present, it is said [to be] "with formation"; when lust is absent, it is said [to be] "without formation." Just as, when a heated iron rod is struck upon wood, it either bends or does not bend — so too, feeling is said to be "with formation" when there is lust, and "without formation" when there is no lust. But when the heated iron rod neither bends nor breaks, so too feeling is then said to be neither "with formation" nor "without formation." Thus, among the five aggregates, one bhikkhu together with the body and the sense-faculties should be understood under the consciousness-aggregate.

As to the elements: there are eighteen elements. Of these, the ten elements that are material — when these are being shown, they should be designated under the form-aggregate, [as] the truth of suffering. And whatever belongs to the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element group should likewise be designated under the consciousness-aggregate, [as] the truth of suffering. But the dhamma-element, being a collection of various dhammas — whether it is found associated with a cause, or disjoined, or subtle, or gross, in whatever way it is apprehended — should be designated accordingly in each case: whether wholesome, or unwholesome, or indeterminate, or unincluded.

As to the twelve bases: the ten material bases should be designated under the form-aggregate, [as] the truth of suffering. Whatever belongs to the mind-base and the mind-consciousness group should be designated under the consciousness-aggregate, [as] the truth of suffering. The dhamma-base is the collection of various dhammas [in the same way].

As to the faculties: whatever dhamma is to be shown among the material faculties should be shown there; whatever is to be shown among the immaterial ones should be shown there — each distinguished separately. In the same way the dhamma-element and the dhamma-base should be distinguished. Just as it is among the dhammas, so it is among the bases — neither less nor more.

As to dependent origination with its factors: there is the forward order, there is the reverse order, there is arising, and there is cessation. Here, in the forward order of arising, the cause is stated thus: conditioned by ignorance [are the formations]; ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense-bases, contact, and feeling are the causes; craving, clinging and becoming are the conditions; then follows birth; and aging-and-death — this should be understood as the forward order [of arising].

132 Peṭakopadesa, Fifth Ground

There it is fourfold: cause, condition, result, and basis. Ignorance, craving, formations, and clinging — this is the cause. Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form; one endowed with sense-desire form is reborn. For one thus reborn there are the six sense bases. Contact and feeling — this is the condition. Whatever is becoming — this is the result. Whatever is birth, and whatever is aging-and-death — this is the basis.

There, dependent origination is twofold: ignorance, formations, craving, and clinging — this is the arising. Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, becoming, birth, and death — this is suffering. And whatever is the cessation of ignorance, the cessation of formations — these, all of them, are cessation. Therefore, in dependent origination, in whatever manner it is to be shown, by that very manner it should be shown.

There are twenty-two faculties: the twelve faculties [beginning with the eye faculty] ... whatever is the faculty of displeasure — this is suffering. The faculty of masculinity, together with view and craving, is its proximate cause. Hence a man should be regarded thus with respect to a man's sensual desire: when internally he is inflamed [with lust] — this is self-conceit; as he is thus inflamed, so it remains externally as well — this is the manner of conceiving. Thus indeed, then the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy become conformable to the faculty of masculinity. When his intention reaches fulfillment, worldly conditions increase the root of the wholesome; but when that intention of his does not reach fulfillment, then the faculty of pain and the faculty of displeasure occur, and the root of the unwholesome increases. But if he has equanimity, becoming one who follows along with the faculty of equanimity, then the root of the wholesome increases through non-delusion. Thus these faculties, unarisen, do not arise; blameless are the feeling-faculty and the masculinity-faculty for one who partakes [rightly] in them.

Then there are the faculties of faith [and so on], up to the faculty of final knowledge — this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Of these, the five faculties beginning with mindfulness have mentality as their proximate cause. The mind-faculty has becoming as its proximate cause. The [remaining] five faculties have materiality as their proximate cause. The faculties of pleasure and displeasure, and the faculty of final knowledge, have the six sense bases as their proximate cause. Then, whichever faculty is able to bring down the discourse or the verse [under discussion], by that very faculty it should be shown. So too with the two elements, with the sense bases, and in every instance of dependent origination. This is the Hāra of Correlation (Otaraṇahāra).

13. Now, what is the Hāra of Purification (Sodhanahāra)?

Three verses connected by a single theme are said to be spoken as one. There, between what has been spoken and what has not been spoken, that which has not been spoken should not be set forth. Why is that? Because indeed, of what has been spoken and what has not been spoken, only that which has been spoken can rightly be set forth. For example: the verse "Heedfulness is the path to the deathless" — this is one verse, and it should be set forth. Why is that? Because there is no other verse on this very theme that has been spoken [elsewhere].

**15. Now what is the discernment of conditions?**

Name-and-form together with its cause, and defilement, together with its cessation — this the understanding takes as its object entirely. The having-a-cause of states should be discerned as to its cause; the having-a-condition of states should be discerned as to its condition.

Now what is the distinction between cause (hetu) and condition (paccaya)? One's own nature is cause; another's nature is condition. What is condition for another's nature may also be cause; what is cause may also, in a certain way, be condition for another's nature. What is not evident is cause; what is evident is condition. What is not mixed with outside things is cause; what is external is condition. One's own nature is cause; another's nature is condition. What produces is cause; what brings to maturity is condition. What is particular is cause; what has come [in from elsewhere] is condition. What is uncommon is cause; what is common is condition. The single one is cause; what follows, one after another, is condition.

The requisite of cause should be fully understood. Arising is cause. Now condition is of two kinds: the condition of what is similar in immediate succession, and the condition of succession (paramparā-paccaya). Cause is likewise of two kinds: the cause of what is similar in immediate succession, and the cause of succession.

Now what is the condition of succession? "Conditioned by ignorance, name-and-form [arises]" — this is the condition of succession. "Consciousness [arises] conditioned by what is similar in immediate succession" — this is the condition of immediate succession. Here, at the beginning, with the cessation of ignorance, does name-and-form also cease? Then, as regards what is similar in immediate succession, for what reason is the condition of succession established as the condition of what is similar in immediate succession?

Now what is the cause of succession? Consciousness, as the cause of succession, is cause; and in another way, as the cause of what is similar in immediate succession, it is cause. For that which, being similar, arises — of that, the cause is indeed the cessation of its very arising; but further, it is the cessation of its mode; the cessation of mode is the cessation of its continuity; the cessation of continuity is the cessation of difference. Thus the two kinds of cause should also be understood.

In dependent origination, just as ignorance is a condition, then again — a condition for what? For unwise attention; and that in turn is the condition for their arising-together; thus it is both condition and arising-together. Now what is the cause there? Just ignorance. For prior to it nothing else is discerned; hence, through the full understanding of ignorance, ignorance itself is cause; the prior is cause, what follows is condition, and that very ignorance is a condition for the arising-together by four ways: by way of the condition of co-arising (sahajāta-paccaya), the condition of immediate succession (samanantara-paccaya), the condition of non-obstruction, and the condition of establishment (patiṭṭhā-paccaya).

140 Petakopadesa, Fifth Section

How is it that, through concealment, ignorance is a condition for formations? Those formations, depending on ignorance, come to growth, increase, and fullness. Just as, for example, a blue lotus or a red lotus, depending on mud, grows and—through being covered—comes to growth, increase, and fullness, so too do those formations, depending on ignorance; through the concealment of ignorance they go to growth, increase, and fullness. Thus, through concealment, ignorance is a condition for formations.

Again, concerning the ripening of action already done and accumulated, it should be understood thus: all of that action, together with its manifold distinctions, is said to be "formations." Thus it is said: "Ignorance is the condition for formations." Again, whether it be the training (of a learner), or merit, or formless attainment, or the state of becoming, or whether it is said "one who has gone beyond," or whether it is not called "a non-returner" and not declared so — for them, what is the condition by which formations [continue to] arise? For them, arising occurs through having not fully eradicated and not fully removed the underlying tendency toward lust that is free from manifest defilement; this becomes the condition for their arising again.

Thus it is said: "Ignorance is the condition for formations." Again, that which is "non-arising" is also [called] formations; for them there remains a residual trace that is not fully eradicated and not fully removed — this becomes a further cause. Through concealment of this kind, "concealment" is the condition for name-and-form. Thus it is said: "Ignorance is the condition for formations."

Again, whatever action leads to re-becoming, all of that is said to be included under the heading of ignorance's formations, combined with craving. 6-1. The five aggregates were taught by the Blessed One — in the discourses, in the Abhidhamma, in questions and answers [illegible].

Herein, what are the five aggregates? The aggregate of form, up to the aggregate of consciousness.

Herein, what is the aggregate of form? The eye and forms, up to the body and tangible objects. This is the aggregate of form.

Herein, what is the aggregate of feeling? Feeling born of eye-contact, up to feeling born of mind-contact. This is the aggregate of feeling.

Herein, what is the aggregate of perception? Perception of forms, up to perception of mental objects — these are the perception-groups. This is the aggregate of perception.

Herein, what is the aggregate of mental formations? Volition regarding forms, up to volition regarding mental objects — these are the volition-groups. This is the aggregate of mental formations.

Herein, what is the aggregate of consciousness? Eye-consciousness, up to mind-consciousness — these are the consciousness-groups. This is the aggregate of consciousness. These are the five aggregates.

Herein, what is full understanding? Knowing [them] as impermanent, as suffering, as non-self — this is full understanding.

Herein, what are the two kinds of form? Visible form and invisible form; form that impinges and form that does not impinge; [illegible] ... conditioned form and unconditioned form. These are the two kinds of form.

What is the meaning of "base" (āyatana) here? In the sense of a resting-place/support, that is the meaning of "base" — just as in the various lairs where snakes, mongooses, and the like take shelter, in whichever shelter they abide in that manner [they are said to dwell] — in just this way, being the support for the conditioned states of that occasion, [the base] is the support for the suffering-dhamma.

Here suffering is to be fully understood, the origin is to be abandoned, cessation is to be realized, and the path is to be developed. **6.** Therein, what is birth? That which, for these and those beings, in this and that order of beings, is birth, being born, descent (into the womb), coming-to-be, the manifestation of the aggregates, the acquisition of the sense-bases — this is birth.
