**6–15.** There are two diseases that are constant: ignorance and craving for existence. For the removal of these two diseases, the Blessed One prescribed two medicines: calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Practicing these two medicines, one realizes two states of freedom from disease: the mind's liberation through the fading away of lust, and the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance. Here, calm is the medicine for the disease of craving; the mind's liberation through the fading away of lust is freedom from that disease. Insight is the medicine for the disease of ignorance; liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance is freedom from that disease.

For thus the Blessed One said: "There are two things to be fully understood: name and form. There are two things to be abandoned: ignorance and craving for existence. There are two things to be developed: calm and insight. There are two things to be realized: knowledge and liberation."

Herein, one who develops calm fully understands form; understanding form, one abandons craving; abandoning craving, one realizes the mind's liberation through the fading away of lust. One who develops insight fully understands name; understanding name, one abandons ignorance; abandoning ignorance, one realizes liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance.

Therefore, when the two things — name and form — have been truly understood, that very understanding means the two things — ignorance and craving for existence — have been abandoned; the two things — calm and insight — have been developed; and the two things — knowledge and liberation — have been realized. By this reason a monk becomes an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. This is the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining. With the exhaustion of his life-span, with the ending of his life-faculty, with its cessation, this suffering ceases, and no other suffering arises. Then, of all these phenomena, their entire non-continuation and non-occurrence — this is the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining.

**6–16.** Herein, what is non-greed as a root of the wholesome? Whatever absence of greed, state of non-greed, non-clinging, lack of longing, lack of craving, lack of covetousness, state of non-desire — this is non-greed, a root of the wholesome. Why is it called a root? Because wholesome bodily action, verbal action, and mental action, together with the associated states such as feeling and so forth, are rooted in non-greed. Or alternatively: the Noble Eightfold Path is called "wholesome," and it is the root of three things. What three? Right intention, right effort, and right livelihood. Since it is the root of these, it is called a root of the wholesome.

Herein, what is non-hatred as a root of the wholesome? Whatever absence of ill-will toward beings or toward formations, absence of malice, non-hatred, state of non-hatred, loving-kindness, or wishing for welfare — this is non-hatred, a root of the wholesome. Why is it called a root? Because wholesome bodily action, verbal action, and mental action, together with the associated states such as feeling and so forth, are rooted in non-hatred. Or alternatively, it is the root of three things. What three? Right view, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Since it is the root of these three things, it is called a root of the wholesome.

**6-17.** Therein, what is the perception of impermanence? Of this, what is the benefit? When the perception of impermanence is developed and cultivated, the mind will not remain attached to any formation in the world, will not cling, but will attain either equanimity or revulsion [turning away]. This is its benefit.

Therein, what is the perception of suffering? "All formations are suffering" — the perception, the perceiving, the discerning with regard to this: this is the perception of suffering. Of this, what is the benefit? When the perception of suffering is developed and cultivated, the mind will not remain in negligence and in slackness, will not cling, but will attain either equanimity or revulsion. This is its benefit.

Therein, what is the perception of non-self? "All phenomena are non-self" — the perception, the perceiving, the discerning with regard to this: this is the perception of non-self. Of this, what is the benefit? When the perception of non-self is developed and cultivated, the mind will not remain attached either inwardly or outwardly, will not cling, but will attain either equanimity or revulsion. This is its benefit.

Therein, what is the perception of foulness? "All formations are foul" — the perception, the perceiving, the discerning with regard to this: this is the perception of foulness. Of this, what is the benefit? When the perception of foulness is developed and cultivated, the mind will not remain attached to the notion of beauty, will not cling, but will attain either equanimity or revulsion. This is its benefit.

**6-18.** These are the four kinds of contemplation taught by the Blessed One: the perception of foulness is the contemplation with regard to the aggregate of form; the perception of suffering is the contemplation with regard to the aggregate of feeling; the perception of non-self is the contemplation with regard to the aggregates of perception and formations; the perception of impermanence is the contemplation with regard to the aggregate of consciousness.

Therein, this [perception] is the opposite of craving; insight (vipassanā) is the opposite of ignorance; mindfulness of the unattractive is the opposite of lust; non-delusion is the opposite of delusion. The perception of impermanence is the opposite of the perception of permanence; the perception of suffering is the opposite of the perception of pleasure; the perception of non-self is the opposite of the perception of self; the perception of foulness is the opposite of the perception of beauty.

Gladness, characterized by delight, is the proximate cause for rapture.
Rapture, characterized by mental satisfaction, is the proximate cause for tranquility.
Tranquility, characterized by workableness, is the proximate cause for happiness.
Happiness, characterized by freedom from affliction, is the proximate cause for concentration.
Concentration, characterized by non-distraction, is the proximate cause for knowledge and vision of things as they really are.
Wisdom, characterized by correct discernment, is the proximate cause for disenchantment.
Disenchantment, characterized by non-attachment, is the proximate cause for dispassion.
Dispassion, characterized by non-adherence, is the proximate cause for liberation.
Liberation, characterized by separation from unwholesome states, is the proximate cause for the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Being dispassionate toward perception, through dispassion for lust connected with form, [there arises] liberation of mind — this is the path of non-returning.

"It is called 'conjoined with that occasion' ['saṃvijjati... velā']": the noble eightfold path is conjoined [with right view, etc.]; because it is conjoined with that, it is said to be "conjoined with that occasion." Then these three fetters are abandoned: for the noble disciple who truly sees, together with right view, these fetters are abandoned, namely — identity-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), and clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbataparāmāsa). With the abandoning of these three fetters, the noble disciple becomes a stream-enterer, not liable to fall into states of woe, certain of reaching full enlightenment.

Herein, what is identity-view? Here the uninstructed worldling… (and so on) … unskilled in the noble Dhamma, regards form as self, …(and so on)… regards consciousness as self — or he regards self as possessing that [aggregate], or that [aggregate] as within self, or self as within that [aggregate]. Dwelling thus obsessed, overcome, with mind possessed by this delusion, taking hold of it again and again, clinging to it with excessive attachment — thus, through improper attention, through a perverted mode of regarding things, this view arises in him unexamined: this is called identity-view.

Then it should be understood that twenty kinds of view arise [in this way]. What twenty? Regarding form as self, regarding self as possessing form, regarding form as within self, regarding self as within form; and likewise for feeling … up to … regarding self as within consciousness. These are the twenty kinds of view that arise. By the abandoning of view, doubt too is abandoned. Thus, through the abandonment of identity-view, these two things no longer occur for the noble disciple. In this way the noble disciple fares well.

He is a trainee (sekha), one of assured destiny, confident, skilled in the noble truths; he does not regard form as self, nor … up to … consciousness as self — for one who sees thus, identity-view does not occur.

Nor does doubt and perplexity occur: thus the noble disciple does not doubt, does not waver, is not uncertain, thinking "Is he indeed the Blessed One?" — this is the state of being endowed with the factor of unwavering confidence in the Dhamma. Likewise he does not doubt nor waver about the Dhamma, thinking "May dispassion, cessation be declared through the fading away of craving" — by this he is endowed with the second factor of unwavering confidence in the Dhamma. The trainee does not doubt … up to … he does not waver about the Community worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world — by this he is endowed with the third factor of unwavering confidence in the Dhamma.

"This is suffering" — he does not doubt, does not waver, has overcome uncertainty. "This is the origin of suffering" — he does not doubt, does not waver. "This is the cessation of suffering" — he does not doubt, does not waver. "This is the noble eightfold path leading to the cessation of suffering" — he does not doubt, does not waver, has overcome uncertainty.

172 Petakopadesa — [Yuganaddhabhūmi]

One should see: "The five aggregates are suffering." Whatever delight, craving, approaching, clinging, wishing, infatuation, longing and aspiration there is for the five aggregates — that is the origin. The abandoning of that is cessation. Calm and insight are the path.

Thus the knowing of these truths occurs at one time, with one adverting, in a single mind-moment, without anything before or after — this is called penetration (abhisamaya). As the Blessed One said: "With the penetration of the truth, three fetters of the noble disciple are abandoned."

Here, when calm and insight are known as a yoked pair (yuganaddha), at one time, with one adverting, in a single mind-moment, how many functions are performed, and of what kind? Suffering is penetrated by the penetration of full understanding; [the origin is penetrated by the penetration of abandoning, cessation by the penetration of realization,] and so on up to: the path is penetrated by the penetration of development.

It illustrates this thus: just as a boat crossing the water, by a single act, performs several functions at once — it brings [the traveller] to the far shore, it leaves the near shore behind, it cuts across the current, and it reaches the landing place — so too, calm and insight, known as a yoked pair, at one time, with one adverting, in a single mind-moment, perform the function of knowing: suffering is penetrated by the penetration of full understanding, and so on up to: the path is penetrated by the penetration of development.

Just as the rising of the sun, at a single moment, without before or after, performs its functions — it dispels darkness, it makes light appear, it reveals forms, and it dries up the dew — so too, calm and insight, known as a yoked pair, at one time ... (as above, in full) ...

Just as a burning lamp, at a single moment, without before or after, performs its functions — it dispels darkness, it makes light appear, it reveals forms, and it consumes its fuel — so too, calm and insight, known as a yoked pair, at one time ... (as above, in full) ...

178 Peṭakopadesa — The Untangling of the Knot

**Which five factors is the first jhāna endowed with?** With initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra), with rapture (pīti), with happiness (sukha), and with one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā). By the arising and occurrence as intrinsic activity of these five factors, the first jhāna is said to be fulfilled in this way. Having arisen possessed of these five factors, one dwells — thus it is said: "Having secluded himself from sense pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion."

**Then the second jhāna, endowed with four factors:** with rapture, with happiness, with one-pointedness of mind, and with internal confidence (ajjhattaṃ sampasādana). Having arisen and become possessed of these four factors, one dwells — thus it is said: "He enters upon and dwells in the second jhāna."

**Then the third jhāna, endowed with five factors:** with mindfulness, with clear comprehension, with happiness, with one-pointedness of mind, and with equanimity. Having arisen and become possessed of these five factors, one dwells — thus it is said: "He enters upon and dwells in the third jhāna."

**Then the fourth jhāna, endowed with four factors:** with equanimity, with purity of mindfulness, with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and with one-pointedness of mind. The fourth jhāna is endowed with these four factors. Thus, by the arising and occurrence as intrinsic activity of these four factors, the fourth jhāna is said to be fulfilled in this way. Having arisen and become possessed of these four jhānas, and having entered upon them, one dwells — thus it is said: "He dwells in a pleasant abiding here and now."

**6–24. Then what is the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā)?** The contemplation of dissolution is the contemplation of impermanence; the contemplation of abandoning, the contemplation of transcending, the contemplation of seclusion, the contemplation of cessation — this is the contemplation of impermanence.

**Then what is the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā)?** The contemplation of affliction is the contemplation of suffering; the contemplation of oppression, the contemplation of urgency (saṃvega), the contemplation of danger — this is the contemplation of suffering.

**Then what is the contemplation of emptiness (suññatānupassanā)?** The contemplation of non-attachment is the contemplation of emptiness; the contemplation of total abandonment, the contemplation of dispassion, the contemplation of cessation — this is the contemplation of emptiness.

**Then what is the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā)?** The contemplation of lack of mastery is the contemplation of non-self; the contemplation of not being under one's control, the contemplation of not being able to act as one wishes, the contemplation of avoidance — this is the contemplation of non-self.

Thus ends the section called "The Untangling of the Knot" in the chapter on the arising of the knowledge of bliss, in the Peṭakopadesa.

**182 Petakopadesa, Seventh Bhūmi**

Just as a bird, before [flying], first makes effort, flapping [its wings], such is the exertion; vitakka is like this. Just as, having spread its wings, it then glides and soars in the sky, maintaining its course, gliding and coasting along — such is vicāra: it keeps following, gliding, coasting.

Vitakka is the full taking hold of the sign of calm, the sign of loving-kindness, [and so on]; vicāra is the sustained holding of the sign of compassion, the sign of non-harming, and the like. Vitakka is non-attention to the unwholesome; vicāra is the guarding of the mind with respect to the wholesome.

Just as one who is full keeps silent, not speaking — such is vitakka; just as one who continually follows after it — such is vicāra. As the unrefined — such is vitakka; as the refined — such is vicāra. What belongs to the gross, coarse stage of concentration is vitakka; what belongs to the subtle, refined stage is vicāra. Unskilfulness regarding states is overcome by vitakka; the knowledge arising from investigation, "this is wholesome, this is unwholesome, this is to be cultivated, this is not to be cultivated" — this too is vitakka; while the steady abiding in what has been investigated and discerned — this is vicāra.

In one who has thus applied vitakka and vicāra, twofold suffering does not arise — bodily and mental; and twofold happiness arises — bodily and mental. Thus the mental happiness born of vitakka and vicāra is called pīti; the bodily happiness is called sukha itself. The one-pointedness of mind therein is called samādhi. This is the first group, comprising the five factors [of the first jhāna].

When one has thereby repeatedly practised, cultivated and made much of that same vitakka and vicāra, one gains mastery therein; then that vitakka and vicāra appear coarse, and likewise the happiness arisen, and the going-out [of mind through the senses] appears coarse. Moreover, the delight and joy born of concentration arise, and the discernment of these [coarse] states comes to be. With regard to this, one who is skilled in reflection, who is well versed in the removal of arisen hindrances, through the fading away of these [coarse factors of vitakka and vicāra], gains inner clarity and singleness of mind. From this comes rapture filled with gladness, which is called joy of mind, and happiness which is called pleasure of mind; this serene, unwavering [state] is called samādhi. This is the second group, comprising the four factors [of the second jhāna]. With the fading away of that rapture as well, one dwells in equanimity, [abandoning delight in it].

Then, being disenchanted with that gladness connected with joy as well, one applies the mind only to equanimity, and, having faded from attachment to that rapture, dwells with equanimity. And just as that happiness free from rapture is experienced with the body, one dwells mindful and clearly comprehending, fully aware. Due to the purity brought by that equanimity together with mindfulness, one abides with equanimity perfected. This is the third group, comprising the four factors [of the third and fourth jhānas].

**[Discussion of the Fourth Jhāna and the Faculties]**

Thus, for the abandoning of bodily pleasure, in the first jhāna the faculty of joy (somanassindriya) ceases. In the second jhāna the faculty of pain (dukkhindriya) ceases. With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the earlier disappearance of joy and grief, he enters upon and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, purified by mindfulness through equanimity.

That [fourth jhāna] is accompanied by equanimity with regard to four faculties: the faculty of pain, the faculty of grief, the faculty of pleasure, and the faculty of joy. Through the cessation of these it becomes conjoined with equanimity. Neither the faculty of pleasure nor the faculty of joy is then present — through the cessation of these it is so. Neither the faculty of pain nor the faculty of grief is then present — through the cessation of these it is so. Thus there is a single faculty of equanimity, [arisen] through the stilling of [all] those [other] faculties. This is called the fourth jhāna.

Herein, for one of lustful temperament (rāgacarita), what is prominent is the faculty of pleasure or the faculty of joy; for one of hateful temperament (dosacarita), what is prominent is the faculty of pain or the faculty of grief; for one of deluded temperament (mohacarita), what is prominent is [the faculty that is] neither painful nor pleasant.

For one of lustful temperament, in the first jhāna [illegible] ceases, and in the second jhāna the other ceases in turn. For one of deluded and hateful temperament, in the first jhāna and in the second jhāna [the corresponding faculty] ceases in turn; [and so] for one of lustful temperament, in the first jhāna and in the second [illegible] likewise ceases — [thus these faculties] cease according to the respective temperament.

For one of lustful and hateful temperament, [the faculties] that have not ceased and that have ceased are [to be understood] accordingly. For one of lustful and deluded temperament, the beginning point of [the faculty] that has not [yet ceased] is to be understood likewise. For one of hateful and deluded temperament, the beginning point of [the faculties] that have ceased and not ceased [is likewise to be understood]...

These are stated as the [modes of] arising according to temperament; and it is further said: by the faculty of joy [arises] the first [jhāna]; by the faculty of pain, the second; by the faculty of grief, the second (?); by the faculty of equanimity, the fourth...

214                                          Petakopadesa — Seventh Section

1. What is to be said regarding generosity (cāga) and wisdom (paññā)? Faith (saddhā) is the serenity of mind; faith is that which has attained unclouded confidence. Why is this so? Because of its characteristic of being unclouded — faith indeed has the characteristic of being unclouded. Others say its characteristic is the arrival at purity of virtues, while yet others say faith has the characteristic of dispelling the murk of doubt.

In another explanation: when one reflects thus about oneself, "I do not know what I am," and being attached to that very attachment — this is called faith. In another explanation: faith is the reflective insight into the danger of views held one-sidedly, and the realization that it is unsettled and without self-nature. By this one attains the first stage, just as one who, looking with the eye into a deep well, sees the water but does not touch it with the body — likewise, there arises the view inclined toward Nibbāna, and that act of resolution — this is called faith. This is the worldly form of faith. In another explanation: by means of noble conduct, one does not settle into views governed by the nature of personality (sakkāya), that conform to birth. One with discernment, understanding reality as it truly is, abandons [these views] through the five faculties of a mild and discerning nature by means of the path of insight; defilements bound up with wrong view are thus abandoned — this too is called faith.

The threshold stage of stream-entry (sotāpatti) is fulfilled in this very stage. In this same stage, the morality of the trainee (sekkha-sīla) is said to be held by the noble ones. In this same stage, tender wisdom is said to occur together with the five faculties. In this same stage, an unshakable resolve is formed — this is generosity (cāga). Therefore faith should be described in terms of resolution through generosity. By a mind inclined otherwise, one whose view is perverse lacks faith; such a person, settling wrongly among various objects, is attached, and thus his faculty of faith becomes corrupted by sensual desire — thereby abandoning the arising of further peaceful and wholesome states, this is resolution through generosity; through the five faculties, resolution through the five; and through virtue (sīla), resolution through calm. These four states together develop virtue — faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom are thus said.

By faith, one crosses over the flood. What is virtue is non-negligence; what is generosity is the result through wisdom. What is wisdom is the five faculties; what is of the five faculties rests in the four factors of stream-entry. What is virtue rests in the faculties of faith. What is generosity rests in various bodily actions. What is wisdom rests in consciousness itself. Mindfulness leads to all good ends. For the trainee, this is the auspicious destiny and the auspicious future state.

For one who attains fullness, performs virtue, and thereby attains fullness, those faculties together with the wholesome root become the ripening of action (kammavipāka). As a summary of these triads: faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom are the four states. Faith and wisdom constitute great good conduct; virtue is good conduct of body and speech; generosity is good mental conduct free from greed — thus when the mind is grasped rightly, the intervening states too become grasped. By these states, good conduct becomes the proximate cause of the path, with reference to the noble truth of suffering.

Regarding the verse: "Above, below, and everywhere released" — herein, what is "above"? That which will be hereafter is the future; this is "above." What is "below"? That which has already passed is the past; this very same [division] is called "below" and "above." Herein, some hold the view of eternalism regarding the past and future aggregates, and some hold the view of annihilationism regarding the present aggregates. Thus these views are twofold: the view of annihilationism and the view of eternalism.

Herein, this is the view of eternalism: by way of these four modes one speaks of eternalism rooted in self-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi): "Form is my self," "Self possesses form," "Form belongs to self" — such clinging to wrong view is what is meant here. And as for the view of annihilationism — it is spoken of in terms of these same modes as annihilationism, saying "This life and this body are not one and the same." Through holding "Form is my self," taking hold of material form as self in these ways, one falls into both annihilationism and eternalism. In regard to each of the five aggregates, the twenty forms of self-view are to be understood accordingly; and in the aggregate-based modes, the view of eternalism and the view of annihilationism are respectively designated.

Petakopadesa — The Seventh Ground (Sattabhūmi)

Therein, one who views thus, "This I am," regards form as self; one regards equanimity and so forth, and the possessor of form as self, and in self the form, or form in self, or self in form — thus the view of equanimity, and so forth. One falls away from the view of a being, and falls away from the prior-end view. One does not regard "This I am." For such a one, the abandoning of all views comes about. In that threefold darkness — regarding the prior end and regarding the posterior end — by that very designation.

Whatever season, friend, among all who are free of passion, does not continue to view "I am" through this reverence, through this effort, through this method. This is the ground of vision and the fruit of stream-entry. For one practiced in noble effort, through the cycle of existence gone to non-being, of those who are 'not to be reborn' — whatever noble effort there is for not being reborn again, whether in the five faculties mild, medium, or strong, all conduces to the abandonment of rebirth. "I" — in view, in desire, in existence, in ignorance, and in the moment.

1. Therein, by the method of teaching there are four truths. By the five faculties and by the fruit of stream-entry, all these are the path and cessation. By the origin of personality-belief, all these are suffering and its origin — this is the method of teaching.

2. Therein, what is investigation? In one who does not regard "This I am," the fetters to be abandoned by vision are abandoned — this is investigation.

3. Therein, what is suitability? There are three kinds of persons: one who has grasped the aggregates by learning, one who has seen the aggregates through insight, and one who is to be guided. The one who has grasped by learning has sharp faculties; following that, the one who has seen through insight has faculties of medium strength; following that, the one with mild faculties is to be guided.

Therein, the one who has grasped the aggregates by learning, through sharpness of faculties, attains the fruit of stream-entry by the path of the ground of vision, and becomes "one-seeded" (reborn only once more). This is the first type of stream-enterer. The one who has seen the aggregates through insight, with mild faculties, attains the fruit of stream-entry by the path of the ground of vision, and becomes a "family-to-family" one (reborn in good families repeatedly). This is the second type of stream-enterer. Therein, the one who is to be guided attains the fruit of stream-entry by the path of the ground of vision and becomes one who is reborn at most seven times. This is the third type of stream-enterer.

Therein, this is the suitability: with mild, medium, or strong faculties, one realizes the ground that is mild, medium, or strong, and through abandoning personality-belief, abandons all wrong views. This is suitability.

4. Therein, what is the proximate cause? Therein, personality-belief is the proximate cause for all wrong views; in personality (existence), name-and-form is the proximate cause; name-and-form is the proximate cause for personality-belief; the five material faculties are the proximate cause for materiality; the six sense bases are the proximate cause for volitional formations.

228                                          Peṭakopadesa, Section on the Right Path

What are the two expositions of it: morality (sīla) which is bodily or verbal good conduct. "In regard to purity" means that in that virtue there should be no disturbance or harm of any kind. Good action as good conduct — this is purity. In this way, up to liberation, in each and every term there are two meanings: the meaning for the person and the meaning for the word. As in this discourse, so in all discourses. There are two kinds of meaning: the ultimate meaning and the highest meaning.

That which, in reliance on the realization of Nibbāna, is to be realized by beings, is called "the remainder that has been accomplished, having been done." This again is to be understood by way of synonym. By this, it should be understood as connected together with its meaning.

Therein, the meaning which the disciple attains is "the gain of which", and this is called "the meaning for the person." Whatever Dhamma the Blessed One teaches, the particular meaning distinguished within that Dhamma — this is "the meaning."

Therein, in virtue, both purity and the benefits [that follow] should be understood. And that benefit is that one does not go to a bad destination, as the Blessed One has said:

"This is the benefit of established in the Dhamma:
One who practices the Dhamma does not go to a bad destination." — this is the meaning.

When a person, in the stage of meditative development, takes up the virtues and becomes endowed with virtue, so it continues up to liberation, as has been explained regarding virtue.

Therein, that which in purity is described by way of the underlying tendencies — that is virtue, and this is the exposition on virtue. Joy, rapture, and tranquility are included under concentration (samādhi) — this is the exposition on concentration. That which, through concentration, knows things as they truly are — this is the exposition on tranquility/wisdom. These three are the powers: virtue, concentration, and tranquility.

Thus virtue is fulfilled; by whatever cause the faculties are purified, by that same cause virtue is fulfilled, and one strives for the non-arising of unwholesome states not yet arisen, for the abandonment of those that have arisen, for the arising of wholesome states not yet arisen, and for the increase of those that have arisen — thus have the faculties been explained. Therein, that which belongs to the exposition on concentration is the faculty of concentration; that which belongs to the exposition on tranquility is the faculty of tranquility. These should be understood as conjoined with each other. Likewise, the striving for the non-arising of unwholesome states not yet arisen is the first right effort; the striving concerning what has arisen is the second; these are the four right efforts, to be undertaken by the four methods. Likewise, the exposition on virtue includes many kinds of action, and so on.

And those thoughts — thoughts free of ill-will, thoughts of non-malevolence, thoughts of non-harming — these, being in common, produce joy in one who delights in them. Is this bodily pleasure a fixed benefit, or does it pass away? This [state without such thoughts] is suffering. Therein, non-distress is concentration. This is the chief cause of tranquility.

Thus, how is the mind defiled: as it does not conflict with and does not increase through wholesome states, the Blessed One teaches this danger, [saying] "therefore, monks, open up [investigate this]," thus having opened up [investigated] the danger, by means of these [various] states the mind is not satisfied, is not pleased by the taste of lust, is not satisfied by hatred, is not satisfied by delusion, is not satisfied by insight. Thus indeed, whatever state obstructs [progress], that very state one should understand. And whatever unwholesome state obstructs [progress], that one should not tolerate.

Another explanation: Whatever these states are, which cannot [be eliminated] in one day — these states, having been taught, are to be seen by the wise. Having distinguished among them, whatever can be taught, having shown that twofold distinction, entering fully into purity, into dispassion, into enlightenment, into the share of enlightenment, into clear knowledge, liberation, and the attainment of full perfection — one enters into wholesome states. Just as, [they say], a blue lotus, a white lotus, or a red lotus, born in water, grown in water, rises up above the water's surface and is undefiled by water — in the same way, having arisen [in defilement], one becomes undefiled [by it], attaining to special knowledge. In this manner one should understand this kind of explanation.

Another: that which is faultless, which is wholesome, not deceitful, fulfilling the higher aim, manifesting what was not manifest before — thus, O monks, [it is said], this unwholesome state will not pursue after and will not appear again. But whatever is faultless, wholesome, not deceitful, fulfilling the higher aim, and which manifests what was not manifest — this mind will not be reckoned among unwholesome states. Thus it should be understood.

1. Herein, by way of the teaching: Here, having taught the ten courses of unwholesome action as [objects of] endurance, and the ten courses of wholesome action as [objects of] endurance, by the unwholesome, [the mind] is not purified — thus it is said: "the defilement of mind is indeed mental defilement."

2. Herein, by way of exposition: there, the undefiled mind, when it becomes polluted, clouded, muddied — like a pool stirred up, muddied, disturbed by mud — so it should be understood.

3. Herein, by way of purification: thus, when the mind is undefiled, when the mind is pure, it enters thoroughly, rightly, into wholesome states — this is called purification.

**4. By the arrangement of terms (padavidhāna):** "Being covered, it is not rained upon" — this is the arrangement of terms for those who are covered, i.e., restrained. "Being uncovered, it is not rained upon" — this is the arrangement of terms for those who are unrestrained. "Having opened up that covering, the opened one is not rained upon" — this is the arrangement of terms belonging to the teaching.

**5. By characteristic (lakkhaṇa):** "Being covered, it is not rained upon" — whatever states have arisen within, born from the defilements, all of these are reckoned together as having one characteristic. "Having opened up that covering, the opened one is not rained upon" — whatever states, outside, arisen without [defilement], all of these share one characteristic and are not rained upon. This is the hāra by way of characteristic.

**6. Herein, what is the hāra of the fourfold array (catubyūha)?** In this sutta, what is the Blessed One's intention? "Whatever unwholesome states are known to anyone, when these have been taught as the governing factors, one will deal with them in accordance with the Dhamma" — this, here, is the Blessed One's intention. This is the catubyūha-hāra.

**7. By turning (āvaṭṭa):** That covering is twofold, arisen from the ground of sense-desire, for one who is given to striving. For him, through lack of reflection, the cankers (āsavā) are born and grow. Through lack of reflection, negligence grows; through negligence, disrespect grows; through disrespect, laxity grows. Concerning this the Blessed One said: "For those who are lax and negligent, the cankers grow." These four arise one from another, and from them the four further arise, and they come to be reckoned as origination. By all these there is suffering and its origin. "Having opened up that covering" — by whatever cause those cankers grow, the abandoning of that cause is the abandoning of the cankers; herein, through diligence, lack of reflection is abandoned, [negligence and disrespect likewise are overcome], and herein the path comes to be developed; therefore the two things, calm and insight, come to fulfilment. That which is the destruction of those cankers — this is cessation. By these, all four [truths] are shown. This is the āvaṭṭa-hāra.

**8. Herein, what is the hāra of analysis (vibhatti)?** "Being covered, it is not rained upon" — this is said categorically. For what reason? Because of the turning back of that very meaning, just as that desire [is turned back] — as it was said by the Blessed One:

"Even though he should do an evil deed
by body, by speech, or by mind,
he is incapable of concealing it —
incapacity [to conceal] is declared of one who has seen the path."¹

Even though the restraining of these [evil deeds] is known, still they are unable to conceal or restrain them. This is the hāra of analysis.

**9. Herein, what is the hāra of reversal (parivattana)?** "Being covered, it is not rained upon" — whatever states there are for one who is uncovered, all these are indeed rained upon; the opened one is rained upon; being rained upon, it is not left unrained-upon. This is the hāra of reversal.

**260 Petakopadesa — Seventh [Section]**

Therein, what is the person who is "bright with a dark destination"? "Bright" means: whatever wisdom ripens him, the states that are contained within it making this world free of darkness — that is called being endowed with the Dhamma rightly heard. Why is it called "wisdom"? Because it is known through wisdom. He knows thus: "These states are wholesome, these states are unwholesome; these states are blameworthy, these states are blameless; these states should be followed, these states should not be followed; these states should be developed, these states should not be developed; these states should be undertaken and dwelt in, these states should not be undertaken and dwelt in; these states should be attended to, these states should not be attended to." But here, through association with a bad friend, through following after a bad friend, he does not become aware of unwholesome states, nor does he come to know wholesome states. Because of that neglect, through lack of attention, through lack of clear comprehension, he follows on heedlessly. Thus he becomes dark, and he goes on to darkness. Being dark, having darkness as his destination, he is indeed one gone to darkness. This is called a person "bright with a dark destination."

Therein, what is the person who is "bright with a bright destination"? It is said thus: this person is closely attached to a good friend, respectfully devoted to him, seeking the wholesome. He approaches the good friend, questions him, inquires of him: "What is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy, what is blameless? What should be followed, what should not be followed? What should be developed, what should not be developed? What should be undertaken and dwelt in, what should not be undertaken and dwelt in? What should be attended to, what should not be attended to? When does defilement occur, when does purification occur? When does engagement occur, when does disengagement occur? When does bondage occur, when does release occur? When does the arising of personality-view occur, when does the passing away of personality-view occur?"

Having been told this, having been instructed in this, being endowed with full comprehension, he knows thus: "These states are wholesome, these states are unwholesome" — and so on — "thus the arising of personality-view occurs, thus the passing away of personality-view occurs." (This should be given in full detail.) Having thus determined which states are to be upheld, seeing with such a mode of vision, he dwells observing accordingly. That person becomes bright, having brightness as his destination. This is called a person "bright with a bright destination."

Therein, what is the person who is "dark with a dark destination"? He contemplates unwholesome states, he utters what is blameworthy; being low and inferior, he dwells immersed in such things. He becomes dark, having darkness as his destination. This is called a person "dark with a dark destination."

Therein, what is that person "dark with a bright destination"? He discerns, among unwholesome deeds, what is unwholesome action. Through an eye established in what is good and wholesome, he becomes aware of unwholesome states and comes to know wholesome states.

And whoever teaches the arising [of a being] among excellent kinsfolk — being foremost in that — he is called by this term: "dark but bound for light" (tamo-jotiparāyaṇa).

And whoever is a person "bright but bound for darkness" (joti-tamaparāyaṇa) — he teaches the result of wholesome kamma. [Yet] that monk, overcome by evil friendship, following after evil companions, inclined toward association with the wicked, develops unwholesome states. Thus he comes to teach rebirth among low kinsfolk. Being foremost in that, he is therefore called "bright but bound for darkness."

And whoever is a person "bright and bound for light" (joti-jotiparāyaṇa) — he, established in brightness, teaches the arising [of a being] among excellent kinsfolk. Being foremost in that, he is therefore called "bright and bound for light."

The one "bright but bound for darkness" teaches the arising of the ten unwholesome states. Of that person, he teaches the result of unwholesome kamma, and he teaches the result of unwholesome states. Of him he teaches wrong knowledge. Of the bright one he teaches wrong view; of the bright one who is "bound for darkness" he teaches the tenfold course of unwholesome kamma. Of the bright one he teaches the exalted state. Of the one "bright and bound for light" he teaches the state free of obstruction. Of the one "bright but bound for darkness" he teaches the state that leads onward. This is the discourse.

1. And what is the Mode of Exposition (Desanāhāra)? In brief, it is a discourse taught summarily. And it is said thus: in brief it is a discourse that teaches wholesome and unwholesome states, teaches the result of wholesome and unwholesome states, and teaches the attaining of favorable and unfavorable destinations. This is the Mode of Exposition.

2–3. And what is the Mode of Investigation (Vicaya-hāra)? Whatever result proceeds from unwholesome kamma, and whatever unwholesome state arises dependent upon it — this is to be understood accordingly. Whatever result proceeds from wholesome kamma, and whatever wholesome state arises dependent upon it — this is to be understood accordingly. This is the Mode of Investigation.

4. And what is the Mode of the Footing (Padaṭṭhāna-hāra)? For whoever is a dark person, his footing is negligence; for whoever is a bright person, his footing is diligence leading to distinction. For the one bright and bound for light, the footing is heedfulness without measure. For the dark one, the footing concerns this world and the next; for the one bright but bound for darkness, the footing concerns both this world and the heavenly world. This is the Mode of the Footing.

5. And what is the Mode of Characteristic (Lakkhaṇa-hāra)? For the one bright but bound for darkness, the characteristic is negligence regarding the states partaking of distinction not yet attained; for the one bright and bound for light, the characteristic is negligence regarding the states partaking of enlightenment not yet attained. For the "bright but bound for darkness" one, this shows itself as heedlessness; for the "bright and bound for light" one, this shows itself as heedfulness without measure. This is the Mode of Characteristic.

**268 Petakopadesa — Seventh Chapter**

[This sutta] teaches the abandonment of craving. This is the abandonment that is rooted in craving. "Enmity in one who dwells heedful" [refers to] sense-pleasure as the state of heedlessness. Through the abandoning of that, one lives heedful, undeluded.

Having abandoned his resentment, he does not long for this world, nor does he long for the world beyond; he does not crave pleasant and agreeable forms bound up with this world, nor does he crave pleasant and agreeable forms bound up with the world beyond. Hence it was said: "He longs not for this world nor for that world."

That abandonment of his is shown, with regard to feelings, as non-confusion, free of distraction. In one who, being undeluded, does not long [for anything], craving [does not arise]; and so, regarding grasping and the desired object, these two matters are shown together. Hence the Blessed One said:

"Not clinging even to this excellent thing,
without expectation, desiring happiness, he lets go."

Of this verse the exposition is twofold: exposition by way of defilement, and exposition by way of purification. Here the exposition given is by way of defilement; thus the exposition of this verse is twofold, to be analyzed by way of defilement and by way of its opposite [purification]. This, then, is the exposition of the verse in its various modes, as has been stated.

1. Herein, what is the teaching? This sutta was taught with reference to craving — [craving that is] harsh and violent — [as in the phrase] "those who are bound to sense-pleasures." This is the intention of the teaching.

2. Herein, what is the investigation? There, the two kinds of defilement are to be thoroughly known through investigation. What are the two? The defilement of sense-pleasure and the defilement of view — these two kinds are to be understood together. This is the investigation.

3. Herein, what is the sutta-recitation? Whatever is said, beginning with "they tremble" and extending to the end — this is the sutta-recitation.

4. Herein, what is the word-analysis? "Beings who tremble, dwelling in the world" — the analysis of this phrase, together with [the phrase] "not grounded [in anything]," is the analysis of the term relating to the world's fear. This, in brief, is also the word-analysis.

"What one intends, what one plans, what one has a latent tendency toward" — this should be explained as occurring in detail,
whether it be a mental, bodily, or verbal action.¹ What is the reason for this?
Since mental factors are indeed volitions, and are said to be "mental action,"² it follows that volition-action
is itself the mental factor, and with this, bodily action and verbal action — these three kinds of action
are declared.

Bodily action and verbal action⁴ are also, when wholesome, that which one grasps at and clings to by body
and by speech; this is called clinging to mere rules and vows (sīlabbataparāmāsa).

As for formations (saṅkhāra), there are three kinds of formations: meritorious formations, demeritorious formations,
and imperturbable formations. Conditioned by these, consciousness has an object as its result,
for the sake of the stability of consciousness.

Perception of pleasure, perception of pain, and perception of neither-pain-nor-pleasure — this is a mental factor. The
grasping of form by which consciousness stands, having form as its object, established in form, delighting in, pursuing,
growing, increasing, and expanding — this is a formation. Thus whatever
is steady among the stations of consciousness, the arising of phenomena by way of an object is called clinging.
This is said to be a mental factor.

The longing, the craving for that which is steady and formless — this too is called a mental inclination.
Attention directed toward agreeable, dear, and pleasant forms — this is a mental factor.

What one intends together with its cause⁵ toward agreeable things is covetousness arising in the body;
resentment toward disagreeable things is ill-will arising in the body. Having gone through all such grounds, this is the falling
of the mind upon the various sensual pleasures and strands of sense desire. Whatever feeling there is, for one
who dwells contemplating gratification in such things, many evil and unwholesome states, formless mental states,
arise. (?) For one whose mind is bound up with lust,⁶ controlled by those defiling sensual desires,
acting according to desire — this is called the planning (or contrivance) in regard to sensual pleasures. Thus all
such mental states have their basis there.

Whoever dwells bound up with those sensual pleasures, desiring and longing for them,
this is called "feeling." For one whose affection and longing⁷ are not yet abandoned, from the change
and alteration of that object there arise grief, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.⁸
Consciousness becomes entangled in suffering, and the mind, overwhelmed, is consumed by the arising of
adverse mental states. This is called "planning" (pakappita).

As to "born of continuity": born of lust, born of continuity, born of hatred, born of delusion — thus is shown the ground of continuity.

7–16

"The four benefits — from the hearing of the Dhamma up to the arising of the higher vision" — this sutta should be explained in detail. One whose faculties have matured, whose wisdom has matured, at the time of death, through rebirth in a heavenly state, attains realization of the solitary enlightenment (pacceka-bodhi).

"One who has heard" (sotāpanna) means: there, from the hearing of the true Dhamma, that is accomplished. And that is also the higher insight-wisdom; through that, craving is worn away, and that is called the irreversible state. This sutta was also taught for the purpose of distinguishing persons: one who follows through faith may have sharp or dull faculties, and one who follows through the Dhamma may have dull or sharp faculties. That person, having right effort, being skilled, is able to attain concentration there, in that meditative state, and having attained that concentrated state of mind, teaches the Dhamma to others for their benefit. But for one who out of malice harms another, that does not bring a good result; rather, it is experienced as painful in this very life, or in a future life, as a result still to be felt.

Therefore, that skilled one, a follower of the Dhamma, has heard the true Dhamma and thereby attains realization. That follower of the Dhamma, of sharp faculties, attains stream-entry. That follower of faith, of dull faculties, attains realization at the time of death. That one of sharp faculties attains it through rebirth in a heavenly state.

"Giving, merit grows" — this verse.

"He is quenched" — this means: it should be understood as the Nibbāna-element without residue. It means the abandonment of the gross defilements. It also means the abandonment of the subtle defilements that remain. Hence there is this saying: "Through the destruction of passion, hatred, and delusion, he is quenched."

"Thereby merit grows, for the restrained one enmity does not arise; the skilled one abandons evil" — this should be understood as mind. "Through the destruction of passion, hatred, and delusion, he is quenched" — this should be understood [as its fruit].

"Thereby merit grows, for the restrained one..." — by these two phrases the mundane wholesome roots should be understood. "Through the destruction of passion, hatred, and delusion, he is quenched" — by this the supramundane wholesome roots should be understood.

"Thereby merit grows — for the restrained one enmity does not arise" — this refers to the preliminary stage. "The skilled one abandons evil" — this refers to the stage of the trainee (sekha). "Through the destruction of passion, hatred, and delusion, he is quenched" — this refers to the stage beyond training (asekha).

"Thereby merit grows — for the restrained one enmity does not arise" — this is to be understood as the course of practice. "The skilled one abandons evil" — the virtue of the trainee. "Through the destruction of passion, hatred, and delusion, he is quenched" — the virtue of the one beyond training.

"Thereby merit grows — for the restrained one enmity does not arise" — by this the teaching of the mundane Dhamma through the tenfold course of virtuous conduct is shown. "The skilled one abandons evil" — the danger in the world is shown. "Through the destruction of passion, hatred, and delusion, he is quenched" — the exposition of the Dhamma as it truly is, is thereby completed.

"Thereby merit grows" — this shows that meaning for one who abstains from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, and so on; thus by the five precepts [this is to be understood]. "For the restrained one enmity does not arise" — through the restraint produced by virtue, he is restrained; and for one so restrained, enmity does not arise. "Through the destruction of passion, hatred, and delusion, he is quenched" — this is said with reference to two [kinds of quenching]. This is the brief explanation.

1. Here, with what purpose is this taught? It is taught so as to show that it applies to gods, to human beings, and indeed to all beings possessed of the five aggregates. These are the two phrases rightly understood. "Thereby merit grows, for the restrained one enmity does not arise, the skilled one abandons evil" — this should be understood as mind. "Through the destruction of passion, hatred, and delusion, he is quenched" — this is spoken of as the two Nibbāna-elements, namely that with residue and that without residue. This is what is taught.

Among these, the portion counted by covetousness (abhijjhā) is the sensual-desire portion (kāma-portion); the portion counted by ill-will is the existence-portion (bhava-portion); the portion counted by wrong grasping (parāmāsa) is the view-portion (diṭṭhi-portion); the portion counted by adherence to "this alone is truth" is the ignorance-portion (avijjā-portion).

These four taints, when they have come to fullness, become floods (ogha) — therefore they are called so. The floods [in turn are]: the sensual-desire portion is the sensual-desire flood, the existence-portion is the existence flood, the ignorance-portion is the ignorance flood, the view-portion is the view flood.

These four floods, having penetrated into the group of latent tendencies, are called "darts" — they remain lodged in the heart. Among these, the sensual-desire flood is the dart of lust (rāga-salla), the existence flood is the dart of hatred (dosa-salla), the ignorance flood is the dart of delusion (moha-salla), the view flood is the dart of [wrong] view (diṭṭhi-salla).

Consciousness, overcome by these four darts, stands fixed on the four [objects] — that is, having made rūpa, vedanā, saññā, and saṅkhāra [its object], consciousness stands there, it is said. Among these, by the dart of lust, consciousness stands entering into the object of rūpa; by the dart of hatred, entering into the object of vedanā; by the dart of delusion, entering into the object of saññā; by the dart of [wrong] view, entering into the object of saṅkhāra.

By these four stations of consciousness, a fourfold bond (ganthi) arises: through lust, through hatred, and through delusion. By lust, the bond of lust arises; by hatred, the bond of hatred arises; by delusion, the bond of delusion arises; by [wrong] view, the bond of [wrong] view arises. Thus this is desire, and these are the defilements — this is the cause of saṃsāra.

Now these are shown in four directions:

[First direction:] Physical nutriment (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra); the perversion "beautiful in the foul"; clinging to sensual pleasure (kāmupādāna); the yoke of sensual desire (kāmayoga); the portion counted by covetousness; the sensual-desire portion; the sensual-desire flood; the dart of lust; consciousness entering the object of rūpa; the bond of lust arising. This is the first direction.

[Second direction:] [Contact-]nutriment; the perversion "happiness in suffering"; clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna); the yoke of existence (bhavayoga); the portion counted by ill-will; the existence portion; the existence flood; the dart of hatred; consciousness entering the object of vedanā; the bond of hatred arising. This is the second direction.

[Third direction:] [Mental-volition] nutriment; the perversion "self in the not-self"; clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna); the yoke of views (diṭṭhiyoga); the portion counted by wrong grasping; the view portion; the view flood; the dart of [wrong] view; consciousness entering the object of saññā; the bond of [wrong] view arising. This is the third direction.

[Fourth direction:] Consciousness-nutriment (viññāṇāhāra); the perversion "permanence in the impermanent"; clinging to doctrines of self (attavādupādāna); the yoke of ignorance (avijjāyoga); the portion counted by adherence to "this alone is truth"; the ignorance portion; the ignorance flood; the dart of delusion; consciousness entering the object of saṅkhāra; the bond of delusion arising. This is the fourth direction.

Thus, these are set forth according to the sutta passages; by the method of illuminating the first direction, this is called the illumination of direction (disālokana).

**314 Petakopadesa — The Eightfold Teaching-Method**

By means of the four perversions (vipallāsa), on the unwholesome side there is "the looking toward the directions"; the defilements are the fetters — this is the ground of the unwholesome side's "looking toward the directions."

In the terms "paṇḍavaṇṇaṃ dassanataṃ sutaṃnahaṃ yāti paṭhamā"¹ and so on — what is the meaning of these terms? There is but one meaning; it is merely a difference of expression. So too for the second, the third, and the fourth. This is the first linking (saṃsajjanā). By this method (peyyāla) all the defilements should be understood under the four terms.

Now, on the wholesome side: the four progresses (paṭipadā), the four jhānas, the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four abidings (vihāra) — the divine, the brahma, the noble, and the equanimous abiding — the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four unshakeable attainments (āneñjappattā dhammā), the four bases (adhiṭṭhāna), the four concentrations (samādhi) — concentration of desire, concentration of energy, concentration of mind, and concentration of investigation — the four dhammas of purity connected with the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), connected with the restraint of the faculties (indriyasaṃvara), leading to the four immeasurables (appamaññā).

Herein, the progress that is painful with swift direct knowledge,² when developed and made much of, fulfills the first jhāna. The first jhāna, when fulfilled, fulfills the first foundation of mindfulness. The first foundation of mindfulness, when fulfilled, fulfills the first abiding. The first abiding, when fulfilled, fulfills the first right effort. The first right effort, when fulfilled, fulfills the first unshakeable dhamma. The first unshakeable dhamma, when fulfilled, fulfills the first base.

The first base, when fulfilled, fulfills the concentration of desire. The concentration of desire, when fulfilled, fulfills the restraint of the faculties. The restraint of the faculties, when fulfilled, fulfills the first immeasurable. Thus, through the restraint of the faculties, the four immeasurables are fulfilled.

Herein: the first progress, and the first jhāna, and the first foundation of mindfulness, and the first abiding, and the first immeasurable, and the first unshakeable dhamma, together with the base, and the concentration of desire, and the restraint of the faculties, and loving-kindness as the immeasurable — this is the first direction.

The second progress, and the second jhāna, and the second foundation of mindfulness, and the second abiding, and the second right effort, and the second unshakeable dhamma, together with the base, the concentration of mind, and compassion as the immeasurable — this is the second direction.

The third progress,⁴ and the third jhāna, and the third foundation of mindfulness, and the third abiding, and the third right effort, and the third unshakeable dhamma, together with the base, the concentration of energy, the factors of enlightenment, and sympathetic joy as the immeasurable — this is the third direction.

316 Peṭakopadesa, Eighth Chapter (Bhūmi)

By the four paths of practice, by the four kinds of knowledge, by the four restraints, by the four abodes, by the four right exertions, by the four... states not conducive to decline, having gathered together [these] dhammas... facing toward insight... by equanimity, by the boundless states — these are the four directions. Having looked at these four directions, this is called "the illumination of the directions," a mode (hāra).

Connecting it thus: the four nutriments, the four paths of practice, the four floods, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four graspings, the four knowledges, the four stages, the abodes, the right exertions, the āsavas and the states not conducive to decline, the dhammas, the bases, concentration together with insight and so on, the four light-giving states, the four... the four boundless states — thus is the connecting by way of the complete distinguishing of wholesome and unwholesome states. This is called the illumination of the directions.

There, the four kinds of purification are to be distinguished with regard to the dhamma that is the division of wholesome and unwholesome, in the first instance. Herein, the purification of stream-entry is the first, of once-returning the second, of non-returning the third, of arahantship the fourth.

There, what are the four kinds of persons? Those persons who have slow direct-knowledge by way of painful progress, and those persons who have quick direct-knowledge by way of pleasant progress.

Of these four kinds of persons: the person who has quick direct-knowledge by way of pleasant progress, and the person who has quick direct-knowledge by way of painful progress — these are two persons. Among these, the one who has quick direct-knowledge by pleasant progress — with reference to one who is unagitated, this person is reckoned as "of calm nature"; with reference to one who is agitated, the person who has slow direct-knowledge by painful progress is reckoned as "fierce." These are the four kinds [of persons thus] known.

There, for the unagitated one there is insight joined with calm; for the calm one there is... insight; for the agitated one there is insight joined with insight itself. Completed.

For the unagitated one the teaching is swift; for the calm one the teaching is moderate; for the agitated one the teaching is moderately swift.

For the unagitated one the penetration is swift; for the calm one the penetration is slow; for the agitated one the penetration is moderate — thus for these persons there are four kinds of progress.

There, this is the defilement: by unwholesome states, by lust, by hatred, by the proliferation arising from these, by defilement, by thought, by attachment — by these, suffering [comes to be] for such a person.

318 Peṭakopadesa — Eighth Section

"Three unwholesome roots": Greed is an unwholesome root, hatred is an unwholesome root, delusion is an unwholesome root.

"Three kinds of contact": contact to be felt as pleasant, contact to be felt as painful, contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

"Three feelings": pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

"Three kinds of examination": examination accompanied by joy, examination accompanied by displeasure, examination accompanied by equanimity.

"Three defilements": greed, hatred, delusion.

"Three thoughts": thought of sensual desire, thought of ill-will, thought of cruelty.

"Three kinds of torment": torment born of greed, torment born of hatred, torment born of delusion.

"Three characteristics of the conditioned": arising, persisting, passing away.

"Three kinds of suffering": the suffering that is itself painful, the suffering of change, the suffering of formations.

Now, from what does greed, the unwholesome root, arise? From a threefold object: the agreeable, the disagreeable, and that which is a basis for equanimity. It is from an agreeable object that greed, the unwholesome root, arises. Thus: with an agreeable object there is contact to be felt as pleasant; dependent on contact to be felt as pleasant, pleasant feeling arises; dependent on pleasant feeling, examination accompanied by joy arises; dependent on examination accompanied by joy, greed arises; dependent on greed, thought of sensual desire arises; dependent on thought of sensual desire, torment born of greed arises; dependent on torment born of greed, arising — the characteristic of the conditioned — arises; dependent on arising, the characteristic of the conditioned, the suffering of change arises.

From what does hatred, the unwholesome root, arise? It is from a disagreeable object that hatred, the unwholesome root, arises. Thus: with a disagreeable object there is contact to be felt as painful; dependent on contact to be felt as painful, painful feeling arises; dependent on painful feeling, examination accompanied by displeasure arises; dependent on examination accompanied by displeasure, hatred arises; dependent on hatred, thought of ill-will arises; dependent on thought of ill-will, torment born of hatred arises; dependent on torment born of hatred, the alteration of what persists — the characteristic of the conditioned — arises; dependent on this alteration of what persists, the characteristic of the conditioned, the suffering that is itself painful arises.

From what does delusion, the unwholesome root, arise? It is from an object that is a basis for equanimity that delusion, the unwholesome root, arises. Thus: with an object that is a basis for equanimity there is contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant; dependent on contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises; dependent on neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, examination accompanied by equanimity arises; dependent on examination accompanied by equanimity, delusion arises; dependent on delusion, thought of cruelty arises; dependent on thought of cruelty, torment born of delusion arises; dependent on torment born of delusion, passing away — the characteristic of the conditioned — arises; dependent on passing away, the characteristic of the conditioned, the suffering of formations arises.

Thus these are the three expositions of the defilements. This is the varied exposition under the heading of the unwholesome.

320 Paṭisambhidāmagga Aṭṭhakathā

Thus there are three unwholesome roots, and also four, and also five; three contacts, three feelings, [and so on] up to perception-and-form — whatever belongs to the unwholesome side, all of it is gathered together within these three unwholesome roots.

Herein, what is the wholesome side? The three wholesome roots; the three kinds of wisdom — wisdom born of learning, wisdom born of reflection, wisdom born of development; the three kinds of concentration — concentration accompanied by thought and examination, [and so on] up to concentration without thought and without examination; the three kinds of training — the training in higher virtue, [and so on], the training in higher wisdom; the three signs — the sign of calm, the sign of exertion, the sign of equanimity; the three kinds of thought — the thought of renunciation, [and so on], the thought of non-harming; the three faculties (described as "attainments") — the faculty "I shall come to know the unknown," [and the rest]; the three kinds of seclusion — seclusion [arising] from renunciation, seclusion from non-ill-will, seclusion from non-harming; the three searches — the search for sensual pleasure, the search for existence, the search for the holy life; the three aggregates — the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom.

Herein, non-greed, which is a wholesome root, fulfils the wisdom born of learning; by the fulfilment of the wisdom born of learning, it fulfils concentration accompanied by thought and examination; by the fulfilment of concentration accompanied by thought and examination, it fulfils the training in higher virtue; by the fulfilment of the training in higher virtue, it fulfils the sign of calm; by the fulfilment of the sign of calm, it fulfils the thought of renunciation; by the fulfilment of the thought of renunciation, it fulfils the faculty "I shall come to know the unknown"; by the fulfilment of that faculty, it fulfils seclusion [born] of renunciation; by the fulfilment of seclusion [born] of renunciation, it abandons the search for sensual pleasure; by the abandoning of the search for sensual pleasure, it fulfils the aggregate of concentration.

Non-hate, which is a wholesome root, fulfils the wisdom born of reflection; by the fulfilment of the wisdom born of reflection, it fulfils the concentration that is without thought but has only examination; by the fulfilment of that concentration, it fulfils the training in higher mind; by the fulfilment of the training in higher mind, it fulfils the sign of equanimity; by the fulfilment of the sign of equanimity, it fulfils the thought of non-ill-will; by the fulfilment of the thought of non-ill-will, it fulfils the [corresponding] faculty; by the fulfilment of that faculty, it fulfils seclusion [born] of non-ill-will; by the fulfilment of seclusion [born] of non-ill-will, it abandons the search for existence; by the abandoning of the search for existence, it fulfils the aggregate of virtue.

Non-delusion, which is a wholesome root, fulfils the wisdom born of development; by the fulfilment of the wisdom born of development, it fulfils the concentration that is without thought and without examination; by the fulfilment of that concentration, it fulfils the training in higher wisdom; by the fulfilment of the training in higher wisdom, it fulfils the sign of exertion; by the fulfilment of the sign of exertion, it fulfils the faculty of "one who has come to know in full"; by the fulfilment of that faculty, it fulfils seclusion [born] of non-harming; by the fulfilment of seclusion [born] of non-harming, it abandons the search for the holy life; by the abandoning of the search for the holy life, it fulfils the aggregate of wisdom.

Thus these three states belong to the wholesome side; all wholesome states are shown by means of these three expositions of knowledge in triads, and the three gateways to liberation are completed therein. Of these, the first is the signless... the second the empty... the third the undesired [or: the first the undesired, the second the empty, the third the signless]. This is called the second exposition of the triad of knowledge.

**322 Petakopadesa, Seventh [Section]**

**4.** Herein, these three persons [are]: the one who understands at once (ugghaṭitaññū), the one who understands through exposition (vipañcitaññū), and the one to be guided (neyya). Of these three persons, the two persons who will attain through the pleasant mode of practice, and having seen [the goal] will be guided by the pleasant mode of practice — these are the [first] two persons. And the two persons who will attain through the painful mode of practice, and having seen [the goal] will be guided by the painful mode of practice — [these are the other two]. These four, by this distinction, become two: one of the nature of [false] view, and one of the nature of craving. These four become three, [and] the three become two. Of these two persons, this is the defilement:

Ignorance and craving; shamelessness and lack of moral dread; lack of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension; the hindrances and the fetters; clinging and adherence [to wrong views]; blindness and delusion; [wrong application of mind] and obstinacy; laziness and unwise attention; doubt and covetousness; not hearing the true Dhamma and not associating with good people.

Herein: ignorance, shamelessness, lack of mindfulness, the hindrances, clinging, blindness, [obstinacy], laziness, doubt, and not hearing the true Dhamma — this is one side.

Craving, lack of moral dread, lack of clear comprehension, the fetters, adherence [to wrong views], delusion, [wrong application of mind], unwise attention, covetousness, and not associating with good people — this is the second side.

Of the ten pairs, the ten [first-named] terms should be taken as the first [group]. By way of the Abhidhamma method, in accordance with the dark [i.e., unwholesome] counterpart, by the same reckoning the [remaining] ten terms of the pairs form the second [group]. This is the second side.

Thus is shown the cessation [arising?] of unwholesome states — this is the origin [samudaya]. That state which one clings to, whether name or form, this is suffering. Thus this is the origin, and this is suffering; by this, both together are suffering and origin. By way of delight-and-lust [nandirāga], the cessation [pamatha-nirodha] should be understood.

What is the wholesome counterpart? Calm and insight; true knowledge and conduct; mindfulness and clear comprehension; moral shame and moral dread, belonging to the bright side; right effort and wise attention; right mindfulness and right concentration; wisdom and liberation; [confidence/firmness] and hearing the true Dhamma; joy and practice in accordance with the Dhamma.

Herein: calm, true knowledge, mindfulness, moral shame, [states] belonging to the bright side, right effort, right mindfulness, wisdom, [confidence/firmness], and joy — these states form one side.

Insight, conduct, clear comprehension, moral dread, [states] belonging to the bright side, wise attention, right concentration, liberation, hearing the true Dhamma, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma — this is the second side.

Thus the wholesome counterpart and the unwholesome counterpart should be understood and stated as [these two] sides, by way of delight-and-lust.
