324 Petakopadesa — Method of the Guide-lines

Those that go to the unwholesome side go to abandonment through the first wholesome [members]; those that are called "unwholesome" go to abandonment by means of wholesome [factors] — thus by the second wholesome side they go to abandonment by means of the second [set of] members. The rest go to abandonment: through dispassion for lust there is liberation of mind; those [members] that belong to the unwholesome side go to abandonment as "second unwholesome," and the unwholesome side goes to abandonment by the first [wholesome] members. The rest go to abandonment: through dispassion for ignorance there is liberation by wisdom — thus it should be understood. This, among the three methods, is the first method, called the Sīhavikkīḷita (Lion's-Play) method.

5. The four members are: "wholesome in mind" and "unwholesome in mind" — these four members are the root-members; one should understand the second, the person. He becomes possessed of these qualities, whether as wholesome roots or as unwholesome roots. Thus these four members, being the former root-members, are to be understood as the four root-members pertaining to the person. This is the Nandiyāvaṭṭa (Nandi-whorl) method. He is possessed of the four qualities — ignorance, craving, calm, and insight. These four qualities are the four root-members — thus it should be understood in all three methods.

Then, by the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, there are four members; thence one's own wholesome [quality] is conjoined with the wholesome side, and in that way with the Nandiyāvaṭṭa [method] again. From the wholesome side thence come nine members [called] "wholesome," thence one's own wholesome is fitting. Thence, by the Sīhavikkīḷita method, there are four members, just as [with] the person, again with the Nandiyāvaṭṭa. These nine members are to be understood as "wholesome."

Then, by the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, there are four members; thence the four root-members converge thus, in due order: calm and insight and release and comprehension of suffering — these four members on the wholesome side bring about convergence with calm. Insight and non-delusion and [illegible] and [illegible] — these four members bring about convergence with insight. These nine members are to be understood as joined with the wholesome qualities.

Then, on the unwholesome side, among the unwholesome members: craving, and delusion, and release, and grasping, and [illegible] — these five members bring about conjunction with craving. Ignorance, and delusion, and [illegible], and [illegible] — these four members bring about conjunction with ignorance. Thus these nine members are to be understood as "unwholesome," joined together. Thus, from this point, it should not be abandoned otherwise. This is the four root-members according to the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method — thus it should be understood.

6. At the time when the four root-members are to be applied by the person according to the method: of the four members belonging to the wholesome [side] — insight, and non-delusion, and [illegible], and [illegible] — these are the four members. Non-delusion(?) and calm and release and [illegible] — these are the four members. Release and grasping and release — these nine members are to be understood as joined among the wholesome qualities.

Then, of the four members belonging to the unwholesome [side]: craving, and delusion, and grasping, and [illegible] — these four members are the root of the unwholesome roots.

Ignorance and delusion, the perception of permanence and the perception of self — this is delusion, this is the teaching.¹ One who applies these root-terms in this way among the unwholesome states — these root-terms free from distortion — when applied also among the wholesome states, should be shown by means of the threefold method.

These root-terms free from distortion are made known through [the method called] "Lion's Play" (sīhavikkīḷita):

Craving and the perception of the beautiful — this is the first distortion.
Greed and the perception of pleasure — this is the second distortion.
Ignorance and the perception of permanence — this is the third distortion.
Delusion and the perception of self — this is the fourth distortion.

Thus these root-terms of the unwholesome are applied in four ways.

Now the root-terms of the wholesome, corresponding to these:

Calm and the perception of the impure — this is the first ground of the opposite.
Non-greed and the perception of suffering — this is the second ground of the opposite.
Insight and the perception of impermanence — this is the third ground of the opposite.
Non-delusion and the perception of non-self — this is the fourth ground of the opposite.

These root-terms free from distortion follow upon [the method of] Lion's Play.

Of these three kinds — whatever ground, whatever heap, or whatever teaching enters into one kind — for that one kind, the unwholesome state and the wholesome state should be discerned by their opposition.³ Having discerned the opposition, whichever kind is to be shown, that kind is shown accordingly. Into one kind another kind does not enter — thus it is to be understood. Into one kind, the root-terms free from distortion enter — thus the understanding of the teaching comes about within the teaching.

Of these three kinds [treated] by the method of Lion's Play, the directions are to be described through four divisions: in the first direction, the first division; in the second direction, the second division; in the third direction, the third division; in the fourth direction, the fourth division.

For the kind called Tipukkhala, the three doors of liberation are to be understood according to direction: in the first direction, the undirected (appaṇihita); in the second direction, emptiness (suññata); in the third direction, the signless (animitta).

For the twofold kind,² liberation of mind through the fading of lust, and liberation by wisdom through the fading of ignorance, are to be understood: in the first direction, liberation of mind through the fading of lust; in the second direction, liberation by wisdom through the fading of ignorance.

These are the kinds. Of these three kinds, the illumination of the root-terms free from distortion — this is called the method of "Surveying the Directions" (disālocana).⁵

Having been illumined thus — "this is this teaching, this is that teaching" — there is right application: on the side of the wholesome and on the side of the unwholesome. This kind is called the "Hook" (aṅkusa). These are the kinds.

330 Peṭakopadesa, Seventh Ground

**[The passage is heavily corrupted in transmission; the following is a best-effort rendering of the recoverable sense, with unclear portions marked.]**

As to "the basis of going" — it is shown in the method as "unwholesome" and as "wholesome," [and as] dependent on training. As to "nika" — it is shown in the method as "wholesome" and as "unwholesome," [belonging] to the subtle [state]. As to "suffering" — it is shown in the method as "wholesome" and as "unwholesome," as a whirlpool of delight (nandiyāvaṭṭa). In regard to these two things, wholesome [and unwholesome], this is the ground where [they are] divided one from another. Or else this very doubt is itself shown among these two. This is called "diversity" (nānatta). In whatever further ways it might be shown in other terms, in that respect it is not shown as a separate ground. It is shown only in terms of non-disclosure. Thus this is the sense: the measure of what is not fully declared is this much.

As to the doubt regarding concentration — it is to be investigated among the various concentrations; [as] discipline-disclosure and non-discipline-disclosure, [or as] undisclosed-by-non-discipline and disclosed [rightly] — this is the measure; it is not a separate concentration.

As to the cessation of diversity in regard to perception — [perceptions] consisting of name, consisting of mechanism (yanta), consisting of hearing (sāvana) — it is shown in those various perceptions. It is not a separate perception [to say that] it is name-made, mechanism-made, or hearing-made. Whatever is the state of non-disclosure among these things — this, it is said, is the measure of diversity.
